download.heading: Get Freedoom (free & open source)

The official, libre release

Freedoom's game data is released under a modified BSD license — you may freely copy, modify, and redistribute it, provided the license and credit travel with it. Grab the official release from the project itself:

Download Freedoom (official site) →

The download contains freedoom1.wad (Phase 1, Ultimate-Doom-style) and freedoom2.wad (Phase 2, Doom-II-style). These are WAD data files, not an executable — you also need a DOOM engine. The simplest free pairing is a small Win32 software-rendering port such as Chocolate Doom or Crispy Doom. Put the port's .EXE and a freedoomN.wad in one folder and run it on your desktop — you don't need any of that to play here, since this page already boots Freedoom for you. Everything involved — game and engine — is genuinely free and open source.

sections.h: How it works & what to expect
sections.html:
Freedoom is not an executable. It's an IWAD: one data file holding every level, sprite, sound and piece of music. An IWAD needs a DOOM engine to run it, and this page ships one — the freely-redistributable DOOM engine running under DOSBox compiled to WebAssembly, with the Freedoom IWAD already sitting beside it. Click play and it boots in a couple of seconds. There is nothing to download, nothing to upload and nothing to configure.

Because it's a 1993-era engine doing 1993-era work, it plays at full speed on anything current. The two campaigns are separate: Phase 1 (freedoom1.wad) is four episodes of nine levels in the style of The Ultimate Doom, and Phase 2 (freedoom2.wad) is a single 30-level campaign in the style of DOOM II.

sections.h: What it is — and what it isn't
sections.html:
Freedoom is not id Software's DOOM, and it isn't trying to copy its art. It's an original, drop-in replacement for the commercial WADs, built from scratch by volunteers so that the open-source engines have something completely free to play. That is exactly what makes it suit a browser: no shareware caveat, no licensing tightrope, no "buy the full version" at level nine.

If you specifically want id's 1993 levels, the DOOM shareware page has them. If you want a free, no-strings DOOM-style shooter to work through, Freedoom is the cleanest option there is.

sections.h: Running it on your own machine
sections.html:
On a desktop you'd pair the same IWAD with a modern source port, and the choice matters:

  • Chocolate Doom or Crispy Doom — software-rendering, tiny, and faithful to the original. The reliable pairing, and the closest thing to what this page runs.
  • GZDoom and other hardware-accelerated ports — these want OpenGL 3.3 and a real GPU pipeline. Excellent natively; not something a browser sandbox can provide.

Put the port's .EXE and a Freedoom WAD in the same folder and most ports will find the IWAD on their own. None of this is needed to play here.

faq.q: Is Freedoom really free and legal to play online?
faq.a: Yes, completely. Freedoom is released under a modified BSD license that explicitly allows anyone to copy, modify and redistribute it. It contains no id Software assets at all, so there are no shareware caveats and no copyright tightrope — the game data and the engine that runs it are both free software.

faq.q: Can I play Freedoom unblocked at school or work?

faq.q: What's the difference between Phase 1 and Phase 2?
faq.a: Phase 1 (freedoom1.wad) is built like The Ultimate Doom — four episodes of nine levels — and works with mods made for the original DOOM. Phase 2 (freedoom2.wad) is a single 30-level campaign in the style of DOOM II, and works with DOOM II and Final Doom mods.

faq.q: Which source port should I use on my own computer?
faq.a: A software-rendering one: Chocolate Doom or Crispy Doom. Both are small, free and faithful to the original. Avoid GZDoom and the other hardware-accelerated ports if you're trying to run them under emulation — they need OpenGL 3.3, which a browser sandbox can't give them. Natively on a desktop, GZDoom is excellent.

Expect to revisit a campaign mission or a small skirmish, not run a competitive late-game match.

You're emulating an x86 CPU inside WebAssembly, which delivers roughly 10–40% of native speed. The original AoE games ran fine on a late-90s Pentium, so a fast modern laptop has headroom — but a busy late-game map with hundreds of units doing pathfinding will feel sluggish, and audio can stutter. Small skirmishes, the campaign tutorial, and menus are the most playable. This is a "revisit it / show someone" experience, not a competitive-multiplayer one.

JezzBall is a 16-bit Windows 3.x program from 1992. That matters here: the everyday default Win32 Wine variant is built for 32-bit apps and usually won't load a 16-bit executable. ExeBrowser ships a dedicated win3x variant for exactly this era of software, and that's the one this page is configured to use. When you load your own JEZZBALL.EXE (or the WEP launcher it came with), pick the win3x runtime.

Mechanically the game is trivial for the emulator: a small playfield, a couple of bouncing balls, and walls that grow when you click. No GPU, no sound-card gymnastics required. If your legally-owned copy starts at all, it generally plays at full, responsive speed — this is about as gentle a workload as Wine-in-the-browser ever sees.

Honest expectation: the blocker is almost never performance — it's getting a legitimate copy in the first place, since Microsoft no longer sells the Entertainment Pack. That's why we've set this page's verdict to partial: the technology works, but you have to bring your own files.

You're given a rectangular room with one or more balls bouncing around it. Click to start building a wall — it grows in both directions from your pointer (vertical or horizontal, toggled with a right-click or the mouse button). When a wall reaches the edges on both ends, it seals off that section; if the sealed-off part contains no ball, it fills in and shrinks the open area.

  • Clear 75% or more of the playfield to finish a level.
  • If a ball hits a wall while it's still growing, you lose a life.
  • Each new level adds another ball and ramps up the speed.

It's deceptively simple and genuinely tense — squeezing the last ball into a sliver of the board is the whole appeal.

1. Click ▶ Play JezzBall above to boot the win3x Wine runtime in this tab.
  2. Use Load your own copy → a folder and select the directory from your legally-owned Entertainment Pack that contains JEZZBALL.EXE.
  3. Make sure the runtime is set to win3x (this page defaults to it) — the 16-bit binary won't start under the default Win32 variant.
  4. If the bundled launcher (WEP.EXE / a pack menu) doesn't cooperate, point the runtime straight at JEZZBALL.EXE instead.
  5. Once the window appears, play with the mouse — click to lay walls, the right button flips wall orientation.

If win3x crashes or hangs on launch, try the r18 variant — it uses an older Boxedwine engine that sometimes handles stubborn 16-bit programs differently.

sections.h: Which Chip's Challenge is this — and why it runs at all
sections.html:
There are really two PC versions, and the distinction matters here:

  • The Microsoft Entertainment Pack build (CHIPS.EXE, 1992) — the one most people remember from Windows 3.1 / 95. It's a tiny 16-bit Windows program that draws with plain GDI: no DirectX, no 3D, no networking. That simplicity is why it's a realistic target for ExeBrowser. Modern 64-bit Windows can't even run it anymore (Microsoft dropped 16-bit support), so a Wine layer is one of the few ways to play the original.
  • The 2015 Niffler re-release (on Steam) — a modernized 32-bit rebuild. It's the version that's now free-to-keep on Steam, but it's a newer build with its own runtime expectations and is better played natively on a real PC.

ExeBrowser targets the 16-bit classic, loaded through the win3x variant — our 16-bit Windows 3.x mode, made for early-1990s apps exactly like this.

Because Chip's Challenge is a turn-based 2D puzzle with no fancy graphics, raw speed isn't a problem — the puzzles don't care that an x86 CPU is being emulated in WebAssembly. The friction is the 16-bit-on-Wine layer:

  • Boots and plays: the board renders, arrow-key movement works, and the level logic is intact. As a puzzle game it's very playable.
  • Rough edges: 16-bit apps under Wine can have palette/redraw glitches, finicky menus, or the occasional refusal to launch. If it won't start cleanly on the first try, that's expected with this era of software.
  • Sound is hit-or-miss: the old MME/PC-speaker audio path may be silent. The game is fully playable muted.
  • No save guarantees: high scores and progress are written to .ini/registry-style files that may not persist between browser sessions. Treat a run as a single sitting.

That's why the verdict is partial, not works great — it's a genuine, playable port of a 30-year-old 16-bit binary, warts and all.

Controls are simple and keyboard-driven:

  • ↑ ↓ ← → — move Chip one tile in that direction
  • Click the game canvas first to capture keyboard input; Esc releases it back to the page
  • Menus (new game, level password, sound) are reachable with the mouse

Steps to play:

  1. Make sure the runtime above is set to the win3x (16-bit Windows 3.x) variant.
  2. Obtain your own copy of the Entertainment Pack CHIPS.EXE (see the licensing box) and unzip it on your computer.
  3. Use “Load your own copy” to drop in the whole folder so CHIPS.EXE finds its companion files.
  4. Click Run in Wine, then click the board and start solving.
  5. If it crashes on launch, try reloading once — and if it still won't go, it may simply be one of the 16-bit titles Wine 1.7.55 doesn't get along with.

16-bit games are the trickiest category in any Wine-based setup, so have a fallback in mind:

  • Easiest legit option: grab Chip's Challenge 1 on Steam — free to keep, runs natively on modern Windows, and is the official port from the rights holders.
  • Preservation reference: the Internet Archive preserves the Windows 3.x version for study; many browsers can play its in-page emulator there too.
  • Other puzzlers that play nicely here: try Minesweeper or JezzBall for quick GDI-era fixes that tend to behave better than 16-bit binaries.

verdict.text: Works well — minimalist, no DirectX needed

intro: Chocolate Doom is the source port built for one purpose: to play exactly like the 1993 original, bugs and all. It's deliberately minimalist — no fancy 3D, no DirectX 9, no launcher bloat — but we don't host it, so this is a bring-your-own-copy guide: load the real Win32 build with the freely-redistributable shareware DOOM1.WAD using the uploader below and it runs on Wine + WebAssembly entirely in this tab. Fair warning: the port's SDL2 rendering is still shaky under browser Wine, so treat it as an experiment — if you just want to be in Knee-Deep in the Dead right now, the hosted DOOM95 build on this page is the one-click route to pixel-faithful, vanilla Doom.

sections.h: Why Chocolate Doom runs so well here
sections.html:
Most modern Doom source ports (GZDoom and friends) lean on OpenGL or DirectX hardware acceleration — exactly the things 32-bit Wine 1.7.55 inside an emulator handles worst. Chocolate Doom goes the other way on purpose. It renders the original 320×200 software framebuffer through SDL and can fall back to plain Windows GDI, with no demand for a GPU or shader pipeline. That low-tech approach is what makes it one of the friendlier games for ExeBrowser: the heavy lifting is just CPU drawing a tiny frame, which the WebAssembly x86 emulator can keep up with comfortably.

It's a 32-bit Win32 executable with no 64-bit dependency, no .NET, and no DRM, so it sits squarely inside what this environment supports.

Chocolate Doom comes in two lineages, and the older one is the safer bet in the browser:

  • 2.3.0 (SDL 1.2) — the last release before the SDL2 rewrite. It does all its drawing in software with the simplest possible video path, which tends to be the most reliable under Boxedwine. Start here.
  • 3.0 and newer (SDL2) — these moved screen scaling into hardware for crisp high-resolution windows. That's great natively but asks more of the emulated graphics layer, so it can be hit-or-miss in a tab. Try it only if the 2.x build misbehaves.

Whichever you load, drop the source-port EXE and DOOM1.WAD into the same folder so the engine finds its game data.

Video: the game itself is featherweight, so the picture should be smooth on a modern laptop. Older Chromebooks and tablets emulate x86 more slowly — playable, but don't expect a perfectly locked frame rate.

Audio: sound is the usual wildcard under Boxedwine. Music and effects may work, stutter, or stay silent depending on your browser and the build; the gameplay is unaffected if audio drops out. The leaner 2.3.0 build is generally the better-behaved one.

Setup screen: Chocolate Doom ships a separate chocolate-setup.exe for key bindings and options. The game runs fine with defaults, so you can skip it — but if you do open it, choose the software/GDI video options rather than anything labeled fullscreen-accelerated.

faq.q: Is Chocolate Doom free and legal to play here?
faq.a: Yes. Chocolate Doom itself is open-source under the GNU GPL v2, so it can be freely redistributed. The game data we load is DOOM1.WAD — the first episode, Knee-Deep in the Dead, released as free shareware in 1993 and still freely redistributable. The registered episodes and Doom II are commercial; buy those from id / Steam and load your own WAD.

faq.q: What's the difference between Chocolate Doom and just running DOOM?
faq.a: Chocolate Doom is a modern recompilation of id's open-sourced engine that intentionally preserves vanilla behavior — same 320×200 look, same limits, same quirks as the 1993 game — while being a clean 32-bit Win32 EXE that's easy to run on today's systems. intro: Jazz Jackrabbit — Epic MegaGames' blisteringly fast 1994 run-and-gun platformer, the one that made a gun-toting green rabbit a DOS-era icon. Here's the honest catch up front: the original game is a DOS program (a 386 protected-mode EXE), and ExeBrowser runs Windows binaries on Wine + WebAssembly, not raw DOS. So the original JAZZ.EXE won't boot here. The good news: the open-source OpenJazz engine is a real Win32 program that loads the original Jazz data files and runs nicely in this player — load it together with the shareware data below and you can play the free levels in a browser tab.

sections.h: Why the original EXE won't run — and what does
sections.html:
Jazz Jackrabbit (1994) is a DOS game: it needs a 33 MHz 386, 4 MB of RAM, and runs in protected mode via a DOS extender. ExeBrowser's runtime is Boxedwine — Wine 1.7.55 plus a 32-bit x86 emulator — which executes Win32 and Win16 Windows programs. It is not a DOS emulator, so it can't load the original JAZZ.EXE. (For straight DOS play, a DOSBox-based site is the right tool.)

The practical route on ExeBrowser is OpenJazz (OpenJazz.exe): a faithful, GPL open-source re-implementation of the Jazz engine, shipped as a small 32-bit Windows executable. It doesn't include any game art or levels — you point it at the original Jazz data files (the shareware set is fine) and it plays them. That keeps everything legal: the engine is free software, and the level data is the shareware you already own.

1. Get a Windows build of OpenJazz from its official releases page (GPL, free).
  2. Get the Jazz Jackrabbit shareware data files from a legitimate archive (or copy them from your GOG install). You want the level data files — the .000 / .j1 resources — plus the shareware levels.
  3. Put OpenJazz.exe and the Jazz data files together in one folder so the engine can find its data.
  4. Click ▶ Play above to boot Wine on this page, then use Load your own copy → a folder and select that folder.
  5. Pick OpenJazz.exe as the entry and click Run in Wine. Click the canvas to capture input.

This is a two-piece setup by design (free engine + your own data). It's a little more fiddly than a one-click game, but it's the honest, legal way to play Jazz in a browser.

sections.h: What to expect: speed, sound, controls
sections.html:
OpenJazz is light and 2D, so it tends to run at full speed in the player even though an x86 CPU is being emulated inside WebAssembly (roughly 10–40% of native, which is plenty for a 1994 platformer). Sound and music depend on the build and your browser, and the original tracker music may not always play cleanly under emulation — gameplay is the reliable part.

Default controls follow the classic layout:

  • ← → run, ↑ aim up / enter doors, ↓ crouch
  • Space or Alt jump · Ctrl fire
  • Enter confirm menus · Esc pause / release the mouse back to the page

If a particular OpenJazz build misbehaves, try the r18 Wine variant from the runtime menu before giving up.

Heretic and Hexen are built on a derivative of the DOOM engine: software-rendered 2.5D, no hardware 3D, no DirectX. That's exactly the kind of workload ExeBrowser's emulated x86 + Wine handles well — frame rates are usually smooth on a modern laptop. The catch is the platform: the games id and Raven shipped in 1994–95 were DOS programs, and there was never an official Win32 build the way DOOM got DOOM95. Run the DOS HERETIC.EXE straight into Wine and it simply won't start.

The fix is a source port. Because Raven open-sourced the engine (GPL, 2008), projects like Chocolate Heretic and Chocolate Hexen rebuilt the original game as a tiny 32-bit Windows EXE that reads the original WAD data. Drop the port EXE and the WAD in one folder, load that folder here, and you get the real, faithful game running in the browser.

sections.h: What you need: the port plus a WAD
sections.html:
This is a two-file job. You supply both pieces; ExeBrowser supplies the runtime.

1. The engineA Win32 source port — Chocolate Heretic for Heretic, Chocolate Hexen for Hexen (free, GPL). Both are small 32-bit EXEs.
2. The game dataThe shareware/demo WAD: HERETIC1.WAD (Heretic shareware) or the Hexen demo WAD. You bring this from a legitimate source — see the box below.
Best Wine variantWin32 (default). If the port misbehaves, try the r18 engine.
Era / originDOS 1994–95; runs here via a modern Win32 source port, not the original EXE.
Expected resultSource port + shareware WAD: plays well. Original DOS EXE alone: will not start.

1. Download a Win32 build of Chocolate Heretic or Chocolate Hexen (the win32.zip from chocolate-doom.org) and unzip it.
  2. Obtain the shareware/demo WAD from a legitimate source (see the licensing box) and copy it into the same folder as the port EXE.
  3. Click ▶ Play above to boot Wine on this page.
  4. Use Load your own copy → a folder and select that folder so the EXE and WAD load together.
  5. Pick the source-port EXE as the entry and click Run in Wine. Click the canvas to capture input.

Heretic adds an inventory (Enter to use, [ and ] to cycle) and the ability to fly and look up/down — a step beyond DOOM's controls.

sections.h: Heretic vs. Hexen — and what's NOT included
sections.html:
Heretic shareware gives you the full first episode, City of the Damned — five levels of elf-vs-undead carnage with the iconic Wand and Phoenix Rod.

Hexen shipped a four-level demo (the start of the Seven Portals hub) rather than a classic shareware episode — it's a free demo, not a full free episode. It also introduced the class system (Fighter/Cleric/Mage) and hub-based puzzle progression.

The registered Heretic episodes, Heretic: Shadow of the Serpent Riders, the full Hexen, and the Deathkings expansion are all commercial — not included and not hosted here. The much later Hexen II is a different beast: it uses the Quake engine (true 3D, hardware acceleration) and is unlikely to run usefully under this 32-bit software-only setup.

faq.q: Can I play Heretic online in my browser for free?
faq.a: Yes, with two free pieces: a Win32 source port (Chocolate Heretic) plus the shareware WAD. The source port is free and GPL-licensed; you supply the shareware WAD from a legitimate source. ExeBrowser then runs the port in your browser via Wine + WebAssembly — nothing to install.

faq.q: Why won't the original Heretic or Hexen EXE run here?
faq.a: Because they're DOS programs, and ExeBrowser runs 32-bit Windows (Win32) programs. There was never an official Windows port the way DOOM got DOOM95. The practical route is a modern Win32 source port that reads the original WAD data — that's a real Windows EXE and runs cleanly.

faq.q: Is it legal to play the Heretic shareware and Hexen demo here?
faq.a: The source-port engine is open-source (GPL). The game data (WADs), however, is still copyrighted by Raven / id and was not given DOOM's explicit free-redistribution license, so we don't host the WADs. Bring your own from a legitimate source like the Internet Archive, or buy the full games on Steam. Avoid cracked or 'full version free' copies.

faq.q: Will Hexen II run in the browser?
faq.a: Almost certainly not usefully. Hexen II runs on the Quake engine — true 3D with hardware acceleration — which is far heavier than the DOOM-style software renderer Heretic and the first Hexen use. ExeBrowser has no DirectX/OpenGL acceleration, so a 3D Quake-engine game is a poor fit.

faq.q: How fast does it run?
faq.a: The engine is lightweight 2.5D software rendering with no DirectX, so once you've loaded a source port it typically plays smoothly on a modern laptop. ExeBrowser emulates an x86 CPU inside WebAssembly at roughly 10–40% of native speed, but DOOM-family games are light enough to feel fine; older Chromebooks and tablets may lag.

intro: Prince of Persia — Jordan Mechner's 1989 game in its 1990 DOS release. The Grand Vizier Jaffar has seized the throne, and the prince has sixty real-time minutes to escape the dungeons, climb through twelve levels of traps and swordsmen, and reach the princess before her time runs out. sections.html: Mechner animated the prince by rotoscoping video of his brother running and jumping, which is why the movement still looks remarkably natural. There is no health bar to refill freely: potions restore one triangle, spikes and long falls kill outright, and the clock never stops. Shift is the key that matters most. It turns a run into a careful step, grabs ledges as you fall, and draws your sword when a guard appears.
Hold Shift and tap an arrow to step right up to the edge of a gap. Ctrl+A restarts the current level at the cost of the time spent. Ctrl+G saves from level 3 onward.

SDLPoP is a faithful open-source (GPLv3) port of the DOS game, rebuilt from a disassembly of the original. It runs natively on Windows, macOS and Linux, adds quicksave and widescreen options, and fixes a handful of original bugs. If you want to keep playing outside the browser, it is the best way to do it.

This is the DOS release of Prince of Persia as preserved in the Internet Archive, running in DOSBox compiled to WebAssembly. The whole game is about 1 MB, so it starts within seconds on a normal connection. Sound and music play once you click into the game.

verdict.text: Partial — the Cadet table can run; launcher, movies and fullscreen are flaky

intro: Full Tilt! Pinball (1995, Cinematronics/Maxis) is the commercial three-table game — Space Cadet, Skulduggery, and Dragon's Keep — that the free Windows Space Cadet was carved out of. It's commercial software we don't host, so this is a compatibility guide: load your own retail copy below and it runs entirely in your browser tab. Same physics engine, same pre-rendered look, just two more tables and a fancier shell. Because it's built on that same well-behaved 32-bit engine, the individual table executables have a real shot under ExeBrowser — but the retail game wraps them in a DirectDraw launcher and intro movies that don't always cooperate with Wine 1.7.55, so set expectations to "fiddly but playable," not "flawless."

sections.h: How it works & what to expect
sections.html:
Full Tilt! ships two builds on the disc: a 16-bit Win 3.x version and a 32-bit Win95 version. The 32-bit build is the one to use here — but its installer is 16-bit and won't run on anything NT-based, so even on a real modern Windows machine people skip the installer and launch the table EXEs directly. Do the same in ExeBrowser.

The good news: the table engine is the same one that powers Space Cadet, which runs well in ExeBrowser. The catch is everything around the table — the FULLTILT.EXE launcher, the pre-rendered intro movies, and the DirectDraw fullscreen mode — which are the parts most likely to show a black screen, a mis-placed window, or to stall under emulation.

AppFull Tilt! Pinball (CADET.EXE / DRAGON.EXE / PIRATES.EXE, or FULLTILT.EXE launcher)
Era1995, 32-bit Win95 build (skip the 16-bit installer)
Best Wine variantWin32 + Gecko — same engine as Space Cadet, whose help/registration screen can prompt for Gecko
How to loadFolder upload — bring the whole game directory so each table finds its .DAT and movie files
Expected resultThe Cadet table is most likely to play; Skulduggery and Dragon's Keep are heavier and may hit DirectDraw issues; movies and fullscreen are the weak points

sections.h: Run the tables directly, and skip the movies
sections.html:
Launch a table EXE rather than the launcher whenever you can — it sidesteps the most fragile DirectDraw code. The retail build accepts a -nomovie switch that skips the pre-rendered intro and drops you straight onto the table, which is exactly what you want under emulation. If ExeBrowser lets you set arguments, add -nomovie after the EXE name; if not, just expect the intro to either play slowly or be skippable with a click or Esc.

  • CADET.EXE — the Space Cadet table (best compatibility bet; it's the engine ExeBrowser already runs well)
  • DRAGON.EXE — Dragon's Keep (medieval fantasy table)
  • PIRATES.EXE — Skulduggery (pirate table)
  • FULLTILT.EXE — the menu launcher; prettier, but the riskiest thing to boot first

Each table needs its own data file (CADET.DAT and friends) sitting beside the EXE, which is why you should upload the whole folder, not a lone executable.

1. Get a copy of Full Tilt! Pinball you legally own — the 32-bit Win95 build from the original retail CD-ROM. ExeBrowser does not provide the game.
  2. On the ExeBrowser home page, set the Wine variant to Win32 + Gecko and click Boot Wine.
  3. Use pick a folder and upload the entire game directory so the .DAT table files and movie assets travel with the EXEs.
  4. Choose CADET.EXE as the entry point first — it's the most reliable. If you can pass arguments, add -nomovie.
  5. Click the canvas to capture input. Launch the ball with the Space bar; the flippers are Z and /. Press Esc to release the mouse.
  6. If a table shows only black or stalls, it's almost certainly DirectDraw fullscreen — try the r18 engine variant, or fall back to the lighter free Space Cadet, which uses the same table and is rock-solid here.

Full Tilt! leans on DirectDraw for its display, and DirectDraw fullscreen is one of the rougher edges of a 1.7.55-era Wine running on a WebAssembly x86 emulator. Even on real Windows 10/11 the game is famous for loading its window half off-screen and mishandling the fullscreen background, so the bar was never high to begin with. Under ExeBrowser you may get a clean Cadet table, or you may get a black launcher, mis-placed window, or a movie that won't advance — it depends on the build and your browser. The pre-rendered tables are not real-time 3D, so the CPU load itself isn't the problem; the display path is. If you want a sure thing, the free Space Cadet extraction of the same Cadet table is the safer, fully-working route.

faq.q: Is Full Tilt! Pinball the same as 3D Pinball Space Cadet?
faq.a: Not quite. Full Tilt! Pinball is the commercial 1995 retail game with three tables — Space Cadet, Skulduggery, and Dragon's Keep. Microsoft licensed only the single Space Cadet table and shipped it as the free 3D Pinball for Windows – Space Cadet with Windows 95 Plus!, 98, 2000, and XP. Same engine and same Cadet table; the retail game just has more of everything.

faq.q: Can I play Full Tilt! Pinball free in my browser?
faq.a: You can play it in ExeBrowser if you own a copy — but the game itself is not free. It's a copyrighted Maxis/EA title that was never released as freeware, so we don't host it and won't link to cracks. If you just want free pinball in the browser, the Space Cadet table is the legitimately-free option.

faq.q: Why does it use the Win32 + Gecko variant?
faq.a: Because it's the same engine as Space Cadet, whose help/registration component can pop a Wine Gecko prompt. Picking Win32 + Gecko bundles Gecko offline so that prompt never interrupts the launch. It does not enable any 3D acceleration — Full Tilt! uses pre-rendered graphics and DirectDraw, not Direct3D.

faq.q: Why is the verdict only 'partial' and not 'works well'?
faq.a: The Cadet table can run, but the retail game's DirectDraw launcher, intro movies, and fullscreen mode are flaky under Wine 1.7.55 — issues it has even on real modern Windows. Expect to launch individual table EXEs directly, skip movies with -nomovie, and accept the occasional black screen. For a guaranteed result, use the free Space Cadet page instead.

faq.q: Why can't I just run the installer?
faq.a: Full Tilt!'s installer is 16-bit and doesn't run on NT-based Windows at all, let alone in this environment. The fix — on real PCs and here alike — is to skip the installer and launch the 32-bit Win95 table executables (CADET.EXE, DRAGON.EXE, PIRATES.EXE) directly from the game folder.

intro:

Same principle either way: your files never leave your device.

The real 7-Zip — Igor Pavlov's free, open-source archiver — running in a browser tab. No download, no install, no account. 7-Zip opens just about every archive format there is: .7z, .zip, .rar, .tar, .gz, .iso and more. It's a small, classic Win32 application, which makes it one of the more reliable tools to run inside ExeBrowser when you need to crack open an archive on a device where you can't install anything. Hit play, point it at your archive, and extract.

sections.h: How it works & what to expect
sections.html:
ExeBrowser runs the actual 7-Zip Win32 binary — the File Manager (7zFM.exe) backed by 7z.dll — inside an x86 emulator and Wine, drawing to a browser canvas. It isn't a JavaScript reimplementation; it's the same program you'd run on Windows. Because everything executes locally in your tab, your archives are never uploaded to a server. The emulator runs at roughly 10–40% of native CPU speed, which is plenty for browsing and extracting; very large or heavily-compressed archives will simply take longer to unpack than they would natively.

App7-Zip File Manager (7zFM.EXE) plus console (7z.exe)
Best Wine variantWin32 (default)
Which buildA 32-bit release — any modern 32-bit 7-Zip is fine
Formats7z, zip, rar, tar, gz, bz2, xz, iso, cab, and more
Getting files outExtract inside 7-Zip, then “Download files written by this app”

ExeBrowser's C:\ drive is in-memory, so 7-Zip can only see what you give it. Put 7zFM.exe, 7z.dll and the archive you want to open into a single folder on your computer, then use Load your own copy → a folder. Inside the 7-Zip File Manager, navigate to your archive, extract it to a subfolder, and use Download files written by this app to pull everything back out as a zip.

  1. Click ▶ Run 7-Zip above to boot Wine on this page.
  2. Load the folder containing 7zFM.exe, 7z.dll and your archive.
  3. Double-click your archive in the file manager, then hit Extract.
  4. Use Download files written by this app to get the extracted files back.

The Wine engine here is 32-bit only, so grab a 32-bit 7-Zip rather than the x64 build (64-bit binaries will not run). The installer is itself an EXE; if you'd rather skip installing, extract the program files with another archiver first and upload just the 7zFM.exe + 7z.dll pair, which is all the File Manager needs to open and extract archives.

sections.h: When to use it vs. a native tool
sections.html: For a single quick extract of a common format, a JavaScript-based extractor running natively in the browser will be faster than emulating x86. 7-Zip in ExeBrowser is the right call when you need its broad format support (some obscure or nested formats only it handles cleanly), want the familiar File-Manager UI, or are already using ExeBrowser for other Windows tools and want one consistent environment.

faq.q: Can I extract a 7z or rar file online without installing anything?
faq.a: Yes. ExeBrowser runs the real 7-Zip File Manager in your browser via Wine + WebAssembly, so there's nothing to install. Bundle 7zFM.exe, 7z.dll and your archive into one folder, load them, extract, then download the results.

faq.q: Is this the real 7-Zip or a clone?
faq.a: It's the real, unmodified 7-Zip Win32 binary running inside an x86 emulator and Wine. ExeBrowser doesn't reimplement it — it runs Igor Pavlov's actual program and renders it to a browser canvas.

faq.q: Are my files uploaded anywhere?
faq.a: No. Everything runs locally in your browser tab. The files you load go into an in-memory C:\ drive that exists only in your session; nothing is sent to a server.

faq.q: Why use 7-Zip here instead of a native browser extractor?
faq.a: For a single common-format extract, a native JavaScript extractor will be faster. Use 7-Zip when you need its broad format support, the familiar file-manager UI, or a consistent environment alongside other Windows tools.

faq.q: Which 7-Zip build should I load?
faq.a: A 32-bit release. The Wine engine is 32-bit only, so the x64 build won't run. Any modern 32-bit 7-Zip works; you only need 7zFM.exe and 7z.dll for the file manager.

WinRAR's GUI loads and behaves like the desktop app — you can browse into an archive, preview the file list, and extract to a folder. Speed sits around 10-40% of native, which is fine for opening and extracting typical archives. The catch is the engine is 32-bit only: recent WinRAR installers default to the 64-bit build, which will not load. Grab an older 32-bit release (the 3.x through 5.x era is plentiful and handles the vast majority of .rar files). If a download only offers an installer, you can often extract WinRAR.exe and its DLLs with 7-Zip on your own machine first and upload just the program folder.

So you need to get both WinRAR and the .rar file you want to open into the upload. The cleanest way: put WinRAR.exe, its DLLs, and your archive in one folder on your computer, then use the pick a folder option. Inside Wine, extract the archive to a subfolder, then use Download files written by this app to pull the results back out as a zip.

A plain text editor, a hex editor, a small calculator, an old file manager — these are single-purpose, decades-old programs that barely touch the parts of Windows that Wine struggles with. Notepad itself is Microsoft software (so bring your own copy), but the wider world of small free utilities runs beautifully here — load any one of them and watch a real .exe open in a browser tab.

sections.h: Why small utilities are the most reliable category
sections.html:
The things that break apps under browser-based Wine are modern GPU features, 64-bit code, recent .NET, DRM, and Win32 APIs added after Windows 7. Small classic utilities use none of that. They draw a plain window with standard controls, read and write files, and quit. That maps almost perfectly onto what Wine 1.7.55 implements well, so the failure rate is very low.

If you've never tried ExeBrowser, run one of these first to get a feel for booting Wine, capturing input on the canvas, and pulling your output back out. The 1995–2008 32-bit Win32 era is the engine's sweet spot, and tiny tools sit right in the middle of it.

sections.html:
A text editor is the perfect demo of getting work in and out. Boot Wine, run the editor, type or open something, then use Download files written by this app to pull the saved file back out of the in-memory C:\ as a zip.

One thing to remember: the virtual drive is wiped on reload, so download before you close the tab. To continue later, re-upload that zip alongside the EXE. A single .exe is usually all you need to load; if a tool asks for DLLs, bundle the whole folder instead.

intro: KeePass is the long-running, free, open-source password manager — and because it is genuinely free to redistribute, the KeePass 1.x Classic build loads here with one click, no download or install needed. One important caveat before you start: it's KeePass 1.x that works here, not 2.x — and there is one big safety caveat too, both covered below. It is GPL software with no activation, no account, and no cloud requirement — exactly the kind of program that runs well under browser-based Wine.

sections.html: There are two KeePass lines, and the difference matters here. KeePass 2.x is built on Microsoft .NET, which browser-based Wine 1.7.55 supports poorly — it usually will not start at all. KeePass 1.x (the "Classic Edition") is a native Win32 program with no .NET dependency, and it is the version to run in your browser. It opens .kdb databases. Note that 1.x and 2.x use different, incompatible database formats: 1.x reads .kdb, while 2.x uses .kdbx. If your vault is a .kdbx file, you would need KeePass 2.x natively to convert or export it first.

sections.h: How to load and save your database

The KeePass 1.x build boots automatically when you press Play. To open your own vault, put your .kdb file alongside it using the folder picker (drop KeePass.exe and your .kdb in one folder and upload that folder), then open the database from inside KeePass with your master password.

KeePass 1.x is a small, lightweight Win32 app, so it runs comfortably at browser-Wine speeds (roughly 10-40% of native). Browsing entries, copying passwords to the clipboard, searching, and editing all feel responsive. The auto-type feature that fills credentials into other Windows programs has limited use here since you are running a single app in a sandbox, but the core vault management — viewing, adding, and editing entries — works as expected.

faq.q: Does KeePass really work in the browser?
faq.a: Yes — KeePass 1.x (Classic Edition) works well because it is a native Win32 program with no .NET dependency. KeePass 2.x, which relies on Microsoft .NET, usually fails to start under browser-based Wine, so stick with the 1.x build that loads here.

faq.q: Is it safe to open my password vault in the browser?
faq.a: ExeBrowser runs entirely inside your browser tab and never uploads your files, so your passwords are not sent anywhere. Still, a vault is your most sensitive file. Use the browser as a convenience for viewing a vault on a machine where you cannot install software — for daily use, run KeePass natively on a trusted device, and always close the tab when done since the in-memory drive is wiped on reload.

faq.q: Can I open a .kdbx file here?
faq.a: No. KeePass 1.x opens the older .kdb format, not the .kdbx format used by KeePass 2.x. The two formats are incompatible. If your vault is .kdbx, you will need KeePass 2.x (natively) to export or convert it to .kdb first.

faq.a: Yes. KeePass is free, open-source software released under the GPL-2.0 license — no purchase, no account, no activation. Because it is freely redistributable, the KeePass 1.x build is hosted here so you can launch it instantly.

intro: Winamp — the player that really whipped the llama's behind — is one of the most nostalgic pieces of late-90s Windows software there is, and this guide covers what happens when you load your own copy here (Winamp's freeware license doesn't let us host it). The classic 2.x and early 5.x builds are small native Win32 programs, so the skinned interface, playlist editor, and equalizer all load under browser-based Wine. Audio playback is the catch: it routes through the emulated Web Audio path, and Winamp's output plugins don't always cooperate. Treat this as a fun nostalgia trip more than a reliable everyday music player.

sections.html:
The classic skinned Winamp window, the playlist editor, the equalizer, and skin loading all tend to render correctly — it genuinely looks like 2001 again. Where it gets shaky is actual sound output: Boxedwine routes audio to Web Audio, and Winamp's output plugins don't always agree with that path. You may get silence or stutter even when the UI is pixel-perfect. The visualizer and any plugins that probe hardware are also unreliable.

Winamp ships as an installer, which won't run well here directly. Install it on a Windows PC (or extract a portable build), then upload the resulting Winamp program folder — winamp.exe plus its Plugins\ and Skins\ folders — using the folder picker. Drop a small MP3 in the same folder if you want to test playback. Stick with the Win32 (default) variant; it's the best fit for a small native player like this.

sections.h: Why audio is the weak spot
sections.html: Everything visual in Winamp is standard Win32 drawing, which Boxedwine handles well. Sound is different: Winamp uses output plugins (the classic out_wave / DirectSound path) that hand audio to the OS audio stack, and Boxedwine has to translate that to the browser's Web Audio API in real time inside an emulator running at roughly 10-40% native speed. That translation isn't lossless — you can hit silence, crackle, or buffer underruns. If playback fails, the UI is still worth a look for the nostalgia alone, and lightweight formats sometimes fare better than high-bitrate files.

faq.q: Does Winamp actually play music in the browser?
faq.a: Sometimes. The interface, playlist, and equalizer load reliably, but audio output is hit-or-miss because Boxedwine has to route Winamp's output plugins through the browser's Web Audio path. You may get clean playback, stutter, or silence depending on the build and file. Treat it as a nostalgia demo rather than a dependable player.

faq.q: Which Winamp version works best?
faq.a: The classic 32-bit builds — Winamp 2.9x or an early 5.x "Lite/Full" — are the sweet spot. They're small native Win32 programs that render the iconic skinned window. Avoid modern 64-bit or DRM-laden builds; ExeBrowser is 32-bit Win32 only.

faq.q: Do you host Winamp for download here?

faq.q: Can I use my old Winamp skins?

intro:
Notepad++ is the much-loved free, open-source code editor — tabbed editing, syntax highlighting for dozens of languages, regex find-and-replace. We host a copy so you can try it, but we'll be straight with you: it does not currently start here. Wine boots it, the plugins load, and then it stops at a "Load langs.xml failed!" dialog with no editor window behind it.

We shipped the config files it asks for (langs.xml and stylers.xml, taken from the matching 7.9.5 source tag) directly alongside the executable, and the dialog still appears — Notepad++ resolves those paths in a way this Wine build doesn't satisfy. The 64-bit builds aren't an option either — the Wine here is 32-bit only.

faq.q: Does Notepad++ work in the browser here?
faq.a: No. It boots and loads its plugins, then stops at a "Load langs.xml failed!" dialog without opening an editor. We're documenting that rather than pretending otherwise.

faq.q: Did you try shipping the missing XML files?
faq.a: Yes — langs.xml and stylers.xml from the matching 7.9.5 source tag, placed beside the executable. The dialog still appears, so the problem is where Notepad++ looks for them under this Wine build, not whether they exist.

sections.h: How it works & what to expect

ExeBrowser runs a 32-bit x86 build of Wine compiled to WebAssembly, so it can execute a real i_view32.exe right in the browser tab. The whole virtual C:\ drive lives in your browser's memory — nothing uploads to a server — which means IrfanView can only see images you bring into that virtual disk. The practical workflow: put the IrfanView program files and the photos you want to view into one folder on your computer, then load the whole folder at once. IrfanView opens, you point it at your pictures, and everything happens locally. Expect roughly 10–40% of native speed; for an image viewer that's typically fine for browsing, zooming, cropping, resizing, and format conversion.

Because the browser-side filesystem starts empty, IrfanView has nothing to open unless you supply it. The cleanest approach is to create one folder containing the unpacked IrfanView program files (i_view32.exe plus its DLLs and any plugin files) and the images you want to work on, then use the pick a folder option so it all lands on the virtual C:\ together. From inside IrfanView you can then browse that folder, open images, batch-convert them to another format, and save the output. Tip: IrfanView's installer can be finicky under Wine (it historically wants MFC42.DLL present), so it's often easier to install IrfanView once on a real Windows PC, copy the resulting program folder, and upload that pre-installed folder rather than trying to run the setup .exe in the browser.

sections.h: What works, and what to skip
sections.html:
Works well: opening and browsing common image formats (JPG, PNG, GIF, BMP, TIFF), zoom and pan, crop/resize/rotate, color adjustments, the thumbnail browser, and batch conversion/rename — the bread-and-butter reasons people open IrfanView. These rely on standard Windows GDI calls that the emulated Wine handles reliably.

  • Plugins: the separate IrfanView PlugIns pack adds extra formats and effects. Some load fine; others (especially ones that hook into media playback) may fail or crash. Treat plugins as bonus, not guaranteed.
  • Video, audio & animation: IrfanView can play media via system codecs, but the WebAssembly Wine has no real multimedia/DirectShow stack. Don't expect video clips or MP3 previews to work.
  • RAW camera files & very large images: may be slow or memory-hungry given the browser sandbox; small-to-medium photos are the sweet spot.
  • Scanning, printing, and "set as wallpaper": these reach for real OS hardware/services that aren't there in the sandbox.

faq.q: Does IrfanView actually run in the browser?

faq.q: Which version of IrfanView should I use?

licenseReason: PuTTY is distributed under the permissive MIT licence, which explicitly allows anyone to use and redistribute it unmodified at no charge, so we can host it.

verdict.text: Partial — the UI launches, but SSH/telnet can't connect in-browser

intro: PuTTY is the classic free, open-source SSH, telnet and serial client for Windows — a single tiny .exe with no installer — and it launches here in one click, with one big caveat: the UI runs, but live SSH and telnet connections can't be made from a browser tab. As a clean 32-bit Win32 program it launches beautifully in ExeBrowser: you get the real configuration dialog, saved-session list, and terminal window, all running on Wine + WebAssembly with nothing to install. The honest catch is networking. A browser tab is sandboxed and cannot open raw TCP sockets, and Boxedwine's emulated socket layer is incomplete, so PuTTY can show you everything up to the moment it tries to reach an SSH server — and then the connection will fail. Treat this page as a way to explore the real PuTTY interface, not as a working remote terminal.

download.heading: Get PuTTY (free, open-source, MIT)
download.html:
The official PuTTY release

PuTTY is released under the permissive MIT licence — free to use and redistribute unmodified, even commercially. Always get it from the author's official site so you can verify the signatures and avoid the many lookalike sites that bundle adware:

Download PuTTY from the official site →

The standalone putty.exe needs no installer — it's a single Win32 binary. Use “Load your own copy” above to drop it in, or hit Play to launch our hosted copy. © Simon Tatham and the PuTTY team; distributed under the MIT licence.

sections.html:
PuTTY is two things stacked together: a tidy Win32 GUI, and a network client underneath it. ExeBrowser nails the first half and can't deliver the second.

  • Launches and renders correctly. The configuration window, the category tree (Session, Terminal, Window, Connection, SSH…), saved sessions, font and colour options, and the terminal window itself all appear and respond as they do on Windows.
  • Networking does not connect. When you enter a host and click Open, PuTTY tries to open a TCP socket. Inside a browser tab that's impossible — the sandbox forbids raw sockets — and Boxedwine's emulated socket support is partial, so the connection times out or errors instead of reaching your server.
  • Serial and local features have nothing real to talk to in the browser either, since there are no host serial ports exposed to the sandbox.

So: great for seeing what PuTTY looks like and how it's configured; not a substitute for a real SSH session.

sections.h: Why the browser can't open the connection
sections.html:
This isn't a PuTTY bug or a Wine quirk you can configure around — it's a hard boundary of the platform. Web pages are only allowed to make network calls through high-level, permission-controlled APIs (HTTP fetches, WebSockets), never raw TCP/IP. PuTTY, like every native SSH client, expects a real socket to the outside world. ExeBrowser emulates an x86 CPU and Wine inside WebAssembly, but it can't hand the program a socket the browser refuses to create. The result is that everything up to the network call works, and the network call itself fails.

If you genuinely need SSH from a browser, the right tool is a server-side web SSH gateway (something the remote host or your hosting provider runs), not a desktop SSH client emulated client-side. For day-to-day use, install native PuTTY — it's a few hundred kilobytes and runs instantly on real Windows.

1. Click ▶ Run PuTTY above to boot Wine on this page, or use Load your own copy and drop in putty.exe from the official download.
  2. The default Win32 variant is correct — PuTTY is a small, well-behaved 32-bit program and needs no special engine.
  3. The PuTTY Configuration dialog appears. Browse the categories, tweak terminal colours and fonts, set up a saved session — all of this works.
  4. Entering a host and clicking Open will not connect, for the socket reasons above. That part is expected to fail in-browser.

Because PuTTY is a single self-contained binary with no DLL dependencies or installer, it's one of the cleaner Win32 apps to launch here — the limitation is purely networking, not compatibility.

faq.q: Can I actually SSH into a server with PuTTY in the browser?
faq.a: No. PuTTY's interface launches and is fully usable, but a browser tab cannot open the raw TCP socket an SSH connection needs, and Boxedwine's emulated networking is incomplete. You'll see the connection attempt fail. For real SSH, install native PuTTY on your computer.

faq.q: Is PuTTY free and legal to run here?
faq.a: Yes. PuTTY is open-source software under the permissive MIT licence, which explicitly allows anyone — including companies — to use and redistribute it unmodified at no charge. That's why we can host a copy directly. You can also bring your own from the official site.

faq.q: Why does the PuTTY window open but connections time out?
faq.a: Everything up to the network call runs in the emulator; the network call itself can't. Browsers only allow controlled APIs like HTTP and WebSockets, never raw TCP/IP sockets, so when PuTTY tries to reach your host the browser refuses and the attempt fails. It's a platform boundary, not a misconfiguration.

faq.q: Where should I download the real PuTTY?
faq.a: Always use the official site at chiark.greenend.org.uk/~sgtatham/putty. Many lookalike sites bundle adware or modified builds. The standalone putty.exe needs no installer — it's a single Win32 binary you can run immediately on Windows.

faq.q: What's the point of running PuTTY here if it can't connect?
faq.a: Mainly to explore and demo the real interface — the configuration tree, saved sessions, terminal appearance, and SSH options — without installing anything. It's useful for screenshots, teaching, or curiosity, but it isn't a working remote terminal.

title: Why FileZilla Can't Connect in a Browser — What to Use
description: FileZilla can't work in a browser — the Wine + WebAssembly sandbox has no outbound networking, so FTP and SFTP can't connect. Here's why, plus alternatives.
keywords: filezilla online, filezilla in browser, run filezilla without install, filezilla web ftp client, filezilla wine, browser ftp client, filezilla no download
ogTitle: Why FileZilla Can't Connect in a Browser — And What to Use Instead
ogDescription: FileZilla is great free software, but an FTP/SFTP client needs real network access — and the browser Wine sandbox has none. We explain why it can't connect and what to use instead.
h1: Why FileZilla doesn't work in a browser (and what to use instead)
author: FileZilla Project (Tim Kosse)

verdict.text: Can't connect — no network in the sandbox

licenseReason: FileZilla Client is free open-source software under the GNU GPL (v2 for older builds, v3 from 3.70.0), so it is legally redistributable — but it can't function here because the browser sandbox provides no real outbound network, so we don't host it to run.
licenseNote: License is fine — the tech is the problem. FileZilla Client is genuinely free, open-source software under the GNU General Public License, so there's nothing shady about it. We're not hosting a playable copy here because it simply can't work in the browser (see below). To use the real thing, download the official client from filezilla-project.org and run it natively on your own machine. Avoid the bundled-adware mirrors that show up in search ads — get it straight from the official site.
intro:
Short version: no, you can't usefully run FileZilla in the browser — and we'd rather tell you that up front than waste your time. FileZilla is a fantastic, free, open-source FTP/SFTP/FTPS client, but it exists to do exactly one thing: open network connections to remote servers. ExeBrowser runs real Win32 programs on Boxedwine (Wine 1.7.55 + a 32-bit x86 emulator compiled to WebAssembly), and that sandbox has no real outbound networking. An FTP client with no network is a window with nothing behind it.

This page exists because people do search for "FileZilla online" and "FileZilla without install," and you deserve a straight answer plus a working alternative — not a fake "launch" button that spins forever.

sections.h: Why it can't connect (the honest breakdown)
sections.html:
Two independent walls stop FileZilla cold here:

  • The Boxedwine WebAssembly build has no working TCP sockets. The emulator's socket layer is incomplete — attempts to configure a connection fail at the kernel level (the log literally reports setsockopt level 0 not implemented), and TCP socket objects don't function. So even before we reach the browser, the emulated Windows networking stack can't open a connection.
  • Browsers don't allow raw outbound connections anyway. Web pages can only talk over HTTP(S) and WebSockets to servers that opt in via CORS. There is no way for sandboxed code to dial an arbitrary FTP server on port 21, an SFTP server on port 22, or an FTPS endpoint. That's a security boundary of the web platform itself, not a Boxedwine bug.

Could someone tunnel FTP over a WebSocket proxy in theory? Yes — but that would require running a relay server, and it still wouldn't be "FileZilla connecting to your host." It's not something this instant-play sandbox does.

sections.h: What about just loading the FileZilla window?
sections.html: Even getting the GUI to paint is shaky. Modern FileZilla (3.x) dropped Windows XP support back at version 3.8.1 and today targets Windows 7, 8, 10 and 11 — newer than the Windows-XP-era API surface Wine 1.7.55 emulates. It's also built on wxWidgets, a heavy UI toolkit that leans on Win32 features old Wine implements unevenly, so crashes on startup are likely. A very old FileZilla 3.8.0-or-earlier build might draw its window — but with networking dead, all you'd get is an empty site manager you can't use.

If you need to move files, here are real options:

  • Install the official FileZilla natively. It's free and open-source. Grab it from filezilla-project.org (avoid ad-laden mirrors) and run it on Windows, macOS or Linux.
  • Use a web-based file manager. Most hosting control panels (cPanel, Plesk) and platforms include a browser file manager and a web SFTP/SSH terminal that work over HTTPS — those are designed for the browser and will actually connect.
  • Try a hosted SSH/SFTP web client your provider offers, which proxies the connection server-side.

For the kinds of self-contained Windows apps that genuinely shine on ExeBrowser — no network needed — see the related links below.

faq.q: Can I run FileZilla in my browser with no install?
faq.a: You can sometimes get an old FileZilla window to appear, but it can't connect to anything. The browser sandbox and the Boxedwine WebAssembly build both lack real outbound networking, so FTP/SFTP/FTPS connections fail. For real use, install the free official client from filezilla-project.org.

faq.q: Why doesn't FileZilla's network connection work under Wine in the browser?
faq.a: Two reasons. First, Boxedwine's WebAssembly socket layer is incomplete — TCP connections fail at the emulated-kernel level. Second, browsers only permit HTTP(S) and opt-in WebSocket traffic, never raw connections to arbitrary FTP/SFTP ports. FileZilla needs exactly those raw connections.

faq.q: Is FileZilla free and legal to use?
faq.a: Yes. FileZilla Client is free, open-source software under the GNU General Public License (GPLv2 for older versions, GPLv3 since 3.70.0 in April 2026). It's completely legitimate to download and use. We just don't host a runnable copy here because it can't function in the browser.

faq.q: Is there any browser-based FTP that actually works?
faq.a: Yes, but not via a desktop FTP client. Use your web host's built-in file manager or web SFTP terminal (cPanel, Plesk, etc.), or a hosted SSH/SFTP web client that proxies the connection server-side over HTTPS. Those are built for the browser; FileZilla is not.

faq.q: Would an older version of FileZilla work better here?
faq.a: A pre-3.8.1 build is more likely to match the older Windows API Wine 1.7.55 emulates, so the window has a better chance of opening. But it makes no difference to connectivity — networking is still dead, so you'd have an unusable empty client either way.

keywords: audacity browser, run audacity online, audacity wine, audacity webassembly, free audio editor browser, audacity 2.4.2 32-bit, edit audio in browser, audacity no download
ogTitle: Can You Run Audacity in Your Browser? Only Old 32-bit 2.x Builds
ogDescription: Audacity 3.x is 64-bit only, so it won't start on ExeBrowser's 32-bit engine. Legacy 2.x builds you load yourself can run for light editing — audio playback and recording are iffy.
h1: Can you run Audacity in your browser?
author: The Audacity Team / Muse Group

verdict.text: Partial — old 2.x editing only, audio iffy

licenseReason: Audacity is open source under the GPL, so it is freely redistributable — but only the legacy 32-bit 2.x builds stand any chance under 32-bit Wine, and we link to the official source rather than re-host an old version.
intro: Audacity is the free, open-source audio editor that millions of people use to trim podcasts, clean up recordings, and chop up tracks — and this page is a compatibility guide for running a copy you load yourself in a browser tab. It is genuinely free software (GPL), so redistribution is allowed — but there is one big catch for browser-based Wine: modern Audacity is 64-bit only. From version 3.0 onward there is no 32-bit Windows build, and ExeBrowser runs a 32-bit x86 engine, so 3.x simply will not start. The only versions that even have a shot here are the legacy 2.x builds (the last being 2.4.2 from 2020), which still shipped a 32-bit installer. Treat this as "load an old version and poke at the editor," not "set up a recording studio in a tab."

sections.h: How it works & what to expect
sections.html:
Audacity is a large wxWidgets application — not a tiny Win32 utility — so even the 32-bit 2.x line is a heavy load for browser-based Wine. Expect a slow first boot while the binary and its DLLs page in. Once it opens, the editing UI (the timeline, tracks, selection tools, effects menus) is the part most likely to work: you can import a WAV/MP3 you bring in, zoom, cut, fade, and apply built-in effects on already-loaded audio.

The shaky part is anything that touches live hardware. Boxedwine routes sound through the browser's Web Audio path, and Audacity's real-time engine (PortAudio) does not always cooperate with that. Recording from a microphone is unreliable to non-functional, and even playback of your edits can stutter or fall silent. So: think of this as an offline audio editor for files you load, with playback as a bonus — not a dependable record/monitor tool.

sections.h: Why you need the old 32-bit build (and where to get it)
sections.html:
This is the make-or-break detail. Audacity 3.0 and everything newer ships only as a 64-bit app on Windows, and ExeBrowser's emulator is 32-bit x86 — a 64-bit .exe cannot even launch. You must use a 2.x release that still offered a 32-bit installer; the final one is Audacity 2.4.2 (2020).

Because Audacity ships as an installer (which runs poorly in this environment), the practical path is: install the old 2.x build on a real Windows PC, then upload the resulting program folder — audacity.exe plus the Languages\, plug-ins\ and DLLs next to it — using the folder picker. Drop a small test WAV in the same folder so you have something to open.

AppAudacity 2.x, 32-bit (e.g. 2.4.2) — not 3.x, which is 64-bit only
Best Wine variantWin32 (default)
Editing UIUsually loads; timeline, cut/trim, and offline effects are the realistic use
Importing filesWAV and basic formats you upload tend to open
PlaybackHit-or-miss — depends on the emulated Web Audio path
Recording from micUnreliable to non-working; don't rely on it
SpeedHeavy app on a ~10–40% native engine — patient, not snappy

If you need real recording, real-time monitoring, or anything from the modern 3.x feature set, run native Audacity on a normal desktop. Here, the win is having a familiar, free editor open in a tab to chop a clip you already have.

faq.q: Can I run the latest Audacity (3.x) in the browser?
faq.a: No. From version 3.0 onward Audacity is a 64-bit-only Windows app, and ExeBrowser runs a 32-bit x86 engine, so a 3.x build cannot launch at all. Only the legacy 32-bit 2.x line (up to 2.4.2 from 2020) can even be attempted here.

faq.q: Can I record from my microphone in Audacity here?
faq.a: Realistically no. Recording depends on Audacity's real-time audio engine reaching live hardware, and Boxedwine's Web Audio routing doesn't reliably support that path. Expect microphone capture to be unreliable or non-functional. Use this for editing files you upload, not for live recording.

faq.q: Is Audacity free and legal to use this way?
faq.a: Yes — Audacity is open-source software released under the GPL, so it is free to use and freely redistributable. We still point you to the official source for the download rather than re-hosting an old version, so you get a clean, unmodified copy.

faq.q: Why is it so slow to start?
faq.a: Audacity is a large wxWidgets application, not a small utility, and ExeBrowser emulates a 32-bit x86 CPU in WebAssembly at roughly 10–40% of native speed. The whole binary plus its DLLs has to page in on first launch, so give it time before declaring it stuck.

faq.q: What's the realistic use for Audacity in the browser?
faq.a: Offline editing of audio you bring in: import a WAV or MP3, then trim, cut, fade, and apply built-in effects. Playback of your edits may work but can stutter. Treat live recording and the modern 3.x features as out of scope here.

title: Why Paint.NET Won't Run in a Browser — What to Use
description: Paint.NET needs the .NET Framework, which browser-based Wine 1.7.55 can't provide — so it won't run here. Here's why, plus a layered editor that does work.
keywords: paint.net browser, run paint.net online, paint.net wine, paint.net webassembly, paint.net linux wine, paint.net alternative browser, mtpaint browser, layered image editor wine
ogTitle: Why Paint.NET Won't Run in a Browser — And What to Use Instead
ogDescription: Paint.NET is built on Microsoft's .NET Framework, which ExeBrowser's 32-bit Wine runtime can't supply. Here's the structural reason it fails, plus a layered image editor that genuinely works in a tab.
h1: Why Paint.NET doesn't run in a browser (and what to use instead)
author: dotPDN LLC / Rick Brewster

verdict.text: Won't run — needs the .NET Framework

intro: Paint.NET is the much-loved free Windows image editor — layers, an undo history, plugins, and a clean interface that sits neatly between MS Paint and Photoshop. We'll be straight with you: it does not run under browser-based Wine, and the reason is structural, not a bug we can patch. Paint.NET is built on Microsoft's .NET Framework — even the old 3.x builds need .NET 3.5 SP1, and 4.x/5.x pile on more — and ExeBrowser's runtime is Wine 1.7.55 on a 32-bit x86 emulator with no .NET Framework installed and no practical way to install one. So this page is an honest "why not," plus a layered editor that genuinely does work in the browser.

sections.html:
Paint.NET isn't a plain Win32 program — it's a managed .NET application. When you launch it, Windows hands control to the .NET Framework runtime (the CLR), which then JIT-compiles and runs Paint.NET's code. No .NET Framework, no Paint.NET. That single dependency is the wall:

  • The runtime isn't here. ExeBrowser ships Wine 1.7.55 with no .NET Framework. Even desktop Wine users install it the hard way with winetricks dotnet35 or dotnet48 — a multi-hundred-MB download plus registry plumbing that simply can't happen inside a range-fetched browser sandbox.
  • Old Wine + .NET is notoriously fragile. Wine's .NET support improved a lot in later releases, but 1.7.55 dates to 2015 and predates most of that work. Even modern Wine struggles: community reports note Paint.NET 4.3.x "runs" but most tools crash the app, 5.1.x has heavy rendering glitches, and 5.2.x crashes on startup outright.
  • It's a 32-bit constraint stacked on a 32-bit constraint. Newer Paint.NET is 64-bit only and uses Direct2D/GPU acceleration — neither of which exists in our 32-bit, DirectX-9-or-older environment.

So even the most Wine-friendly classic 3.x build would face down a missing CLR. We'd rather tell you that up front than have you upload an installer that spins and dies.

If you want a real raster image editor running in the browser right now, reach for mtPaint. It's a small, fast, native Win32 painting program — no .NET, no DirectX — so it loads and runs under our default Wine variant. You get layers, palette and indexed-colour editing, selections, gradients, and clean PNG/GIF/JPEG export. It's not a Paint.NET clone, but for pixel art, quick edits, retouching, and format conversion it covers most of the same ground and actually works.

For freehand sketching and a slightly more modern feel, GrafX2 and MS Paint are also worth a look. For anything that needs Photoshop-grade layer compositing, you're better off on a native desktop install of Paint.NET itself.

sections.h: Where to get the real Paint.NET
sections.html: If you do want Paint.NET, run it on a real Windows machine — that's where it shines. It's free to download and use, but it is not open source: it was MIT-licensed only until late 2007, the source was then restricted, and since v3.5 (2009) it has been proprietary freeware. The license permits free use and unmodified redistribution but forbids modifying or creating derivative works, so we don't host it here. Always download it from the official site, getpaint.net, to avoid the bundled-adware fakes that crowd search results.

faq.q: Can I run Paint.NET in my browser with ExeBrowser?
faq.a: Not reliably. Paint.NET depends on Microsoft's .NET Framework, which our browser-based Wine 1.7.55 runtime doesn't include and can't realistically install. The app needs the CLR to start, so it won't launch. For an in-browser image editor, use mtPaint instead.

faq.q: Why does Paint.NET need the .NET Framework?
faq.a: Paint.NET is a managed .NET application, not a plain Win32 program. Its code runs on the .NET Common Language Runtime, which must be present before the app can start. Classic 3.x needs .NET 3.5 SP1; 4.x and 5.x require newer, heavier .NET versions. None of those ship in ExeBrowser's environment.

faq.q: Is Paint.NET open source or free to redistribute?
faq.a: Paint.NET is free to download and use, but it is not open source. It was MIT-licensed until 2007, then the source was restricted, and since version 3.5 (2009) it has been proprietary freeware. The license forbids modifying it or making derivative works, so we don't host it — get it from the official site, getpaint.net.

faq.q: Does Paint.NET work on Linux or Wine at all?
faq.a: Only with effort and lots of caveats, and not in a browser. On a full desktop Wine install you can install the .NET Framework via winetricks, but even then tools frequently crash, newer versions glitch or fail to start, and there's no official Linux support. Our browser runtime can't install .NET, so it won't run here regardless.

faq.q: What's the best browser image editor that actually works?
faq.a: For raster editing in the browser via ExeBrowser, mtPaint is the strongest pick — it's a native Win32 editor with layers, palette control, and clean export, and it runs under the default Wine variant. GrafX2 and MS Paint are good lighter options.

licenseNote: We don't host Paint.NET. It's free to use but proprietary (not open source), and its license doesn't grant us redistribution rights. Download it only from the official site, getpaint.net — and note it requires a real Windows install with the .NET Framework, which this browser runtime can't provide.
licenseReason: Proprietary freeware since v3.5 (2009) — free to use and redistribute unmodified, but modification/derivatives are forbidden and we have no clear right to host it.

author: Mark Tyler / wjaguar (mtPaint project)

licenseNote: mtPaint is GPL-licensed open-source. The current Windows build is 64-bit with GTK2 DLLs — bring your own copy using Load your own copy above, or try an older 32-bit build from the SourceForge page.

verdict.text: Works well

intro: mtPaint (Mark Tyler's Painting Program) is a tiny, fast, open-source raster editor built for icons, pixel art, and quick photo touch-ups — and this guide covers running your own copy of it in a browser tab. The whole program is only a few hundred kilobytes and was designed to run happily on a 200 MHz machine with 16 MB of RAM — which is exactly the kind of lightweight, native Win32 software that runs well under browser-based Wine. If you want to push pixels, edit an indexed palette, or crop and resize an image on a Chromebook or a locked-down PC with nothing installed, mtPaint is one of the most dependable choices in ExeBrowser. Load your copy below, let Wine boot, and you have a real paint program in a browser tab — nothing installed, nothing uploaded to a server.

sections.h: How it works & what to expect
sections.html:
mtPaint is a small, self-contained Win32 application. It draws a standard window with standard toolbars, reads and writes image files on the local virtual C:\ drive, and never reaches for DirectX, 3D acceleration, recent .NET, or post-Windows-7 APIs. That is precisely the profile Wine 1.7.55 handles cleanly, so the default (Win32) variant is all you need.

Expect a snappy, no-frills editing experience: brush, pencil, fill, shape, and selection tools; zoom for pixel-precise work; palette and channel editing; and the usual crop, resize, rotate, and flip operations. Because everything runs locally in WebAssembly at roughly 10–40% of native speed, small images feel instant. Very large photos will redraw more slowly than on a real PC, but the tiny footprint keeps things responsive for the icon-and-sprite work mtPaint is built for.

sections.h: Opening images and saving your work
sections.html:
The in-browser C:\ drive starts empty and is wiped every time you reload, so the workflow is: bundle the mtPaint program folder with any images you want to edit into one folder, load it, then open your file from inside mtPaint. (If you use the hosted copy below, it boots ready to go — just create a new canvas or drop your own images alongside it.)

When you're finished, save inside mtPaint first — it exports PNG, GIF, BMP, JPEG, TIFF and more — then click Download files written by this app to pull your saved images out of the virtual drive as a zip. The golden rule of ExeBrowser applies here: download before you close the tab, because the virtual disk does not survive a reload.

sections.h: What it's great at (and what it isn't)
sections.html:
mtPaint shines at pixel art, sprite sheets, icon and favicon work, indexed-palette images (great for retro and GIF-style art), and fast crop/resize/recolor jobs. The palette editor and indexed-color tools are genuinely good and hard to find in modern editors.

It is not a layered photo compositor like Photoshop or GIMP — it favors a single working image and a flat, fast workflow. There's no GPU filtering, no RAW pipeline, and no plugin ecosystem. None of that is a Wine limitation; it's simply mtPaint's deliberately minimal design. For its intended job — pushing pixels quickly — it runs in the browser about as reliably as anything we host.

faq.q: Is mtPaint free to use in the browser?
faq.a: Yes. mtPaint is open-source software released under the GNU General Public License (GPL), so it is completely free to use, modify, and redistribute. We host a clean copy here, and running it in your browser costs nothing.

faq.q: Does mtPaint run well under browser-based Wine?
faq.a: It does. mtPaint is a small native Win32 program that uses standard windowing and avoids DirectX, 3D, and modern .NET, so it maps almost perfectly onto what Wine 1.7.55 implements well. Use the default (Win32) variant — it's one of the more reliable graphics editors in ExeBrowser.

faq.q: Can I edit my own images?
faq.a: Yes. Load your image files alongside the mtPaint folder, open them from inside the app, edit, save in your chosen format (PNG, GIF, BMP, JPEG, TIFF and more), then use Download files written by this app to retrieve them. Always download before reloading — the virtual drive is wiped on refresh.

faq.q: Is mtPaint good for pixel art?
faq.a: Very much so — pixel art and icons are exactly what it was built for. The zoom, single-pixel pencil, fill, and indexed-palette tools make it a favorite for sprites, favicons, and retro-style art. It's not a layered photo editor like GIMP, but for pixel work it's hard to beat for the size.

faq.q: Why is mtPaint so small and fast?
faq.a: By design. The whole program is only a few hundred kilobytes and was written to run on hardware as modest as a 200 MHz CPU with 16 MB of RAM. That tiny footprint is also why it boots and responds quickly inside the WebAssembly Wine sandbox.
