verdict.text: Works well (windowed SDL build)

intro: GrafX2 is the legendary free, open-source 256-color pixel-art editor — a spiritual successor to Amiga's Deluxe Paint, beloved by demoscene and game-art folks for its palette tools, gradients, custom brushes and Lua scripting. It's a small, SDL-based Win32 program with no DirectX or .NET dependency, which makes it a genuinely good fit for browser-based Wine. We don't bundle it here, but it's free (GPL) and easy to get: grab the Win32 build from the project page, load grafx2.exe with the uploader below, and it runs entirely in your tab — draw, then pull your image back out as a PNG without installing anything.

sections.h: How it works & what to expect
sections.html:
GrafX2 renders through SDL, not DirectX or modern Direct3D, so it sidesteps the graphics APIs that trip up browser-based Wine. The 32-bit Windows build is exactly the kind of self-contained Win32 app ExeBrowser handles best: it boots into its palette-driven UI, the tools respond, and you can paint, fill, set gradients and edit the 256-color palette as normal.

Two honest caveats. First, run it windowed — GrafX2's fullscreen mode change can be flaky under emulation, so if you hit a black screen, drop back to a window. Second, you're running an x86 CPU emulated inside WebAssembly at roughly 10-40% of native speed; GrafX2 is light enough that this is fine for normal pixel pushing, though very large canvases or heavy Lua scripts will feel slower than on the desktop.

sections.h: Get the SDL1 32-bit build for best results
sections.html:
The project ships several Windows packages. For browser-Wine, prefer the SDL (version 1) 32-bit portable build over the newer SDL2 one — the older SDL1 stack is what Wine 1.7.55 understands most reliably. Grab the portable ZIP (no installer needed), unzip it, and load the whole folder so grafx2.exe finds its data files.

  • Open the SDL 32-bit (win32) portable archive, not the installer or the 64-bit build (this engine is 32-bit only).
  • Keep the program folder intact — config, fonts and skins live alongside the EXE.
  • It saves in .png, .gif, .bmp, .pcx and many retro formats; PNG is the safe everyday choice.

sections.h: Saving your art out of the browser
sections.html:
Files you create live in the sandbox, so save your work, then use ExeBrowser's Download files written by this app button before you reload or close the tab. That zips up everything the program wrote — including your saved PNGs — and downloads it to your computer. If you skip this step, the sandbox is wiped on reload and your image is gone.

Step by step

  1. Click ▶ Run GrafX2 above to boot Wine on this page (keep Win32 (default)).
  2. If prompted, download the GrafX2 SDL 32-bit portable ZIP and unzip it.
  3. Use Load your own copy → a folder and select the unzipped GrafX2 directory.
  4. Pick grafx2.exe and click Run in Wine (stay in windowed mode).
  5. Draw, save your image, then click Download files written by this app to get the PNG out.

faq.q: Is GrafX2 free to use?
faq.a: Yes. GrafX2 is free, open-source software released under the GPL-2.0-only license. The original MS-DOS version was developed by Sunset Design from 1996-2001 and later released as open source, and it remains actively maintained. You can download, use and redistribute it freely.

faq.q: Does GrafX2 actually run in the browser?
faq.a: Yes, and well. It's a small SDL-based Win32 program with no DirectX, Direct3D or .NET dependency, so it runs cleanly under browser-based Wine. Use the SDL1 32-bit portable build and run it windowed for the most reliable experience.

faq.q: Which GrafX2 download should I use here?
faq.a: Use the SDL (version 1) 32-bit portable Windows build. Avoid the 64-bit build (this engine is 32-bit only) and prefer SDL1 over SDL2, since the older SDL stack is the most compatible with Wine 1.7.55. The portable ZIP needs no installer.

faq.q: How do I get my drawing off the page?
faq.a: Save your image inside GrafX2 (PNG is easiest), then click Download files written by this app in ExeBrowser. That zips up everything the program wrote and downloads it. Do this before reloading — the sandbox is cleared on refresh.

faq.q: Why does GrafX2 feel a bit slow sometimes?
faq.a: ExeBrowser emulates an x86 CPU inside WebAssembly, giving roughly 10-40% of native speed. GrafX2 is lightweight enough that ordinary pixel work is comfortable, but very large canvases, big zoom levels or heavy Lua scripts will run slower than on a real desktop.

verdict.text: Partial — UI loads, audio is unreliable

licenseNote: We don't host foobar2000 here. It's freeware, but not open-source — its license only permits redistributing the unmodified official installer, and the build you'd run in-browser is an extracted program folder, which isn't covered. Get it from the official foobar2000 site (older 32-bit builds live at foobar2000.org/old), and only run a copy you obtained legitimately.
intro: foobar2000 is the famously lightweight, no-nonsense audio player that power users have loved for over two decades — tiny, fast, infinitely configurable. This is a bring-your-own-copy compatibility guide: foobar2000's license doesn't let us host an extracted build, so you load your own copy below and it runs client-side. The catch for browser-based Wine is twofold: the current 2.x release is built for modern 64-bit Windows, and even the older 32-bit builds have a long history of audio-output trouble under Wine. The interface generally renders, so you can poke around the playlist and preferences, but treat actual music playback as unreliable rather than a daily driver. This is a "look how far emulation has come" demo more than a real listening setup.

sections.h: What works, and what to expect
sections.html:
Two things matter here. First, version: foobar2000 2.x targets 64-bit Windows and a modern toolchain that browser-based Wine (Wine 1.7.55, 32-bit only) can't handle. You'll want a legacy 32-bit build from the 1.x series, available at foobar2000.org/old. Second, audio: even on full desktop Wine, foobar2000 is notorious for listing no output device, emitting static, or going silent depending on the audio driver. Boxedwine routes sound through Web Audio, which is an even narrower path, so playback is genuinely hit-or-miss.

What does tend to work is the UI: the main window, the playlist, the Preferences dialog and its dense option tree, and basic file browsing. That alone is enough to relive the interface — just don't count on hearing anything.

foobar2000 ships as an installer, which won't run cleanly in-browser. The reliable approach is to install a legacy 32-bit 1.x build on a real Windows PC (or use a portable install option if the version offers one), then upload the resulting program folder — foobar2000.exe plus its components\, user-components\, and config files — using the folder picker. Drop a small test track (an MP3 or FLAC) into the same folder so you have something to try.

Once it's loaded, open Preferences → Playback → Output and try each device option (Primary / Default) — that's the single most useful knob if you get any sound at all.

sections.h: Why audio is the weak link
sections.html: foobar2000's whole design philosophy is a thin player with a pluggable output stack — and that stack is exactly what struggles under emulation. Output plugins probe for audio hardware and expect a specific driver model; Boxedwine presents an emulated path to Web Audio that those plugins weren't written for. The result, well-documented across years of WineHQ and Linux forum threads, ranges from clean playback (rare and version-dependent) to silence, stutter, or harsh static. Advanced features — ReplayGain scanning, DSP chains, visualizations, and anything touching networking or online services — are even less likely to behave.

faq.q: Can I really run foobar2000 in a browser?
faq.a: You can load and explore it. A legacy 32-bit foobar2000 build will boot under ExeBrowser's Wine + WebAssembly and show its real interface, playlist, and preferences. Audio playback, though, is unreliable under emulation, so think of it as a working demo of the UI rather than a dependable music player.

faq.q: Why doesn't the latest foobar2000 work?
faq.a: The current 2.x releases are built for 64-bit Windows and a modern toolchain. ExeBrowser runs Wine 1.7.55 with a 32-bit x86 emulator, so it needs an older 32-bit build — grab one from the official old versions page.

faq.q: Will my music actually play?
faq.a: Sometimes, but don't count on it. foobar2000 has a long, well-documented history of audio problems under Wine — no output device listed, static, or silence — and the browser audio path is even narrower. The interface loads reliably; sound is the part that's hit-or-miss.

faq.q: Do you host foobar2000 for me to click and play?
faq.a: No. foobar2000 is freeware but closed-source, and its license only allows redistributing the unmodified official installer — not the extracted program folder you'd run here. Download it yourself from the official site and upload your own copy.

faq.q: Is there a better-working media app to try in the browser?
faq.a: For nostalgia, classic Winamp behaves similarly (UI yes, audio iffy). If you mainly want something that reliably runs, small Win32 utilities and the bundled classic games are a safer bet — see the compatibility guide for what holds up under emulation.

h1: Why VLC doesn't work well in a browser (and what to use instead)
author: VideoLAN
licenseReason: VLC is free and open-source (GPLv2 player / LGPLv2 libVLC), so it is legally redistributable, but its bytes are not hosted here yet — bring your own copy from VideoLAN.

verdict.text: Open-source & legal, but video playback won't work well

intro: VLC media player is the legendary open-source player that opens almost any video or audio file. It's free, GPL-licensed, and completely legal to run anywhere — but here's the honest part: ExeBrowser emulates a 32-bit x86 CPU inside WebAssembly at roughly 10–40% of native speed, with no GPU video acceleration. VLC is built to decode and push pixels fast, so even when the interface loads, actual playback tends to stutter, tear, or fail outright. This page exists to set expectations truthfully and point you at what really works.

sections.h: How it works & what to expect
sections.html:
ExeBrowser runs the real vlc.exe Win32 binary on Wine 1.7.55 compiled to WebAssembly. There's no driver doing hardware video decode, no DirectX/Direct3D output, and no GPU — every frame would have to be decoded on an emulated CPU running far below native speed. For a media player, that's the worst-case workload.

What you may see, in practice:

  • The UI sometimes loads. A 32-bit classic build (the 0.9–1.1 era) has the best odds of the window even appearing, since modern VLC is 64-bit-first and far heavier.
  • Playback usually doesn't. Even when a file opens, video typically stutters, shows a black frame, or throws errors like libvlc.dll failed to initialize. Audio-only files have slightly better odds but still aren't reliable.
  • Modern 64-bit VLC won't run at all. ExeBrowser is 32-bit Win32 only. Grab a 32-bit (win32) build if you want to even reach the interface.

For reference, VLC carries only a "silver" rating on Wine's own application database on native Linux with real GPU drivers — and Boxedwine has neither the GPU nor native CPU speed. So set your expectations very low: this is a curiosity, not a way to actually watch a movie in a tab.

sections.h: Why a media player is the hardest case for browser-Wine
sections.html:
The things ExeBrowser is great at — lightweight Win32 apps, old games, utilities, document editors — all have one thing in common: they don't need to decode 30+ high-resolution frames per second in real time. VLC does. Three layers stack against it here:

  • No hardware acceleration. Native VLC leans on your GPU for decode and rendering. The emulated environment has neither, so everything falls back to the slow software path.
  • Emulated CPU speed. At ~10–40% of native, software decoding of anything beyond a tiny, low-bitrate clip simply can't keep up.
  • Missing system codecs & output modules. VLC's video-output modules expect DirectX/Direct3D or OpenGL surfaces that Boxedwine doesn't provide.

Together, these mean even a perfectly legal, perfectly installed VLC will struggle. It's not a licensing limit — it's physics and the emulator.

If you actually want to watch something:

  • Use your browser's own player. Modern browsers play MP4/H.264, WebM, and MP3 natively with hardware acceleration — just open the file or drag it into a tab.
  • Install real VLC on your device. It's free and open-source for Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, and iOS from videolan.org. On the desktop it'll run circles around any emulated copy.
  • Stay in ExeBrowser for the right tools. Lightweight utilities and old games are where browser-Wine shines — see the related pages below.

faq.q: Can I actually watch videos in VLC through the browser here?
faq.a: Realistically, no. ExeBrowser emulates a 32-bit CPU in WebAssembly with no GPU or video acceleration, so even when the VLC interface loads, video typically stutters, shows a black frame, or fails to initialize. It's a fun experiment, not a working media player. To actually watch something, use your browser's built-in player or install real VLC on your device.

faq.q: Is VLC free and legal to run?
faq.a: Yes. VLC is open-source — the player is GPLv2 and the libVLC engine is LGPLv2 — so it's free to use and freely redistributable. The legal status is not the problem here; the emulator's lack of GPU and native speed is. Download it free from videolan.org.

faq.q: Why won't modern (64-bit) VLC run at all?
faq.a: ExeBrowser runs 32-bit Win32 software only. Current VLC ships as a 64-bit-first build that the emulator can't load. If you want the interface to even appear, you'd need an older 32-bit (win32) build, but playback still won't perform well.

faq.q: Which VLC version has the best chance of opening?
faq.a: A classic 32-bit build from the 0.9–1.1 era is lighter and is most likely to at least show its window. VideoLAN keeps these in its official archive at download.videolan.org. Even so, expect the UI at best — not smooth playback.

faq.q: What can I run in ExeBrowser instead that actually works?
faq.a: Lightweight Win32 utilities and classic games are the sweet spot. Try a text editor, a calculator, a paint tool, or any of the old games linked below — they don't need real-time video decoding, so they run far better than a media player.

intro: The classic Microsoft WordPad — the rich-text editor that sat between Notepad and Word on every Windows PC from Windows 95 onward — can run in a browser tab via Wine + WebAssembly, provided you load your own copy: it is not free to redistribute, so we don't host it. WordPad is a lightweight Win32 app, so the basics behave: typing, fonts, bold/italic, bullets, and saving .rtf files all work. Bring your own wordpad.exe from a Windows PC you own and load it above — and note that Microsoft removed WordPad from Windows 11 24H2, so if you want something free and built-in, jump straight to AbiWord.

sections.h: How it works & what to expect
sections.html:
ExeBrowser boots Wine 1.7.55 on a 32-bit x86 emulator compiled to WebAssembly, then runs the actual wordpad.exe binary you load — no re-implementation, no upload to a server. WordPad is tiny and makes no use of DirectX, .NET, or 64-bit code, so it starts quickly and the editing surface is responsive.

What works: typing, font and size selection, bold/italic/underline, text color, bullet and number lists, paragraph alignment, and opening and saving .rtf and .txt files. That covers what most people actually use WordPad for.

What's rough: Wine's rich-text engine isn't pixel-perfect. Saving to .doc usually falls back to RTF, and opening old .doc or legacy Write .wri files often shows garbled characters with no formatting. Treat this as a capable plain-and-rich-text scratchpad, not a Word replacement.

sections.h: Bring your own copy (and which file to load)
sections.html:
WordPad isn't a free download, so there's no honest one-click version to host. To run the genuine article, copy it off a Windows PC you own:

  • Windows 10 / older Windows 11: grab C:\Program Files\Windows NT\Accessories\wordpad.exe. The write.exe launcher in C:\Windows just forwards to it, so copy both if you want either entry point.
  • Windows 11 24H2 or newer: WordPad was removed entirely, so copy it from an older machine or a backup — there is no legitimate place to download it.

Once you have the file, click Run WordPad above, choose Load your own copy, and select wordpad.exe. The player uses it as the entry point automatically.

If the licensing dance is annoying — or your PC simply doesn't have WordPad anymore — the open-source AbiWord is a genuinely better fit for the browser. It's freely redistributable, reads and writes .rtf, .doc, and its own formats far more faithfully than Wine's RTF engine, and we can offer it as instant-play with nothing to copy. For plain text, Notepad or the cross-platform Notepad++ load instantly too.

faq.q: Can I run WordPad online for free with no download?
faq.a: You can run it in your browser here with no install, but WordPad itself isn't a free download — it's proprietary Microsoft software bundled with Windows. You supply a wordpad.exe copied from a Windows PC you own and load it above. If you want something free with nothing to copy, use AbiWord instead.

faq.q: Where can I download WordPad?
faq.a: There's no legitimate standalone WordPad download — Microsoft only ever shipped it inside Windows, and it was removed from Windows 11 version 24H2 (October 2024). Sites offering a "WordPad installer" aren't official. Copy wordpad.exe from a Windows machine you already own, or pick a free editor like AbiWord.

faq.q: Does WordPad open .doc files correctly in the browser?
faq.a: Not reliably. Basic .rtf and .txt open and save fine, but Wine's rich-text engine often shows garbled characters with lost formatting for old .doc and legacy .wri files, and saving to .doc usually falls back to RTF. For real Word documents, AbiWord handles them far better.

faq.q: Why was WordPad removed from Windows?
faq.a: Microsoft deprecated WordPad in 2023 and removed it from all editions starting with Windows 11 version 24H2 to cut maintenance of legacy code that hadn't seen meaningful updates in years. It recommends Word for rich text and Notepad for plain text. That's exactly why running an old copy here, or switching to AbiWord, can be handy.

faq.q: Will WordPad run fast in the browser?
faq.a: Yes, comfortably. WordPad is a small Win32 app with no DirectX or 3D, so even at the 10–40% of native speed you get from x86-on-WebAssembly emulation, typing and formatting feel responsive on a modern laptop.

licenseReason: Classic calc.exe is proprietary Microsoft software covered by Windows licensing; the 2019 MIT-licensed Calculator release is the modern UWP app, not this Win32 binary, so it is not redistributable.
intro:
The old Windows calc.exe — the plain four-function-and-scientific calculator from Windows 95 through Windows 7 — is just about the perfect thing to run under browser-based Wine. It's a tiny, single-purpose Win32 program that draws a standard window, does some arithmetic, and quits. No GPU, no 64-bit code, no .NET, no networking — none of the things that trip up the emulator. It boots in seconds and behaves exactly as you remember.

One catch: it's Microsoft software, so we can't hand you the file. If you own Windows, you already have calc.exe; copy it across and upload it, and it runs cleanly on the everyday Win32 variant.

sections.h: Why the classic calculator is a great first thing to run
sections.html:
If you want to see ExeBrowser work with the least possible friction, the classic calculator is an ideal demo. It belongs to the most reliable category of all: small, decades-old Win32 utilities that barely touch the parts of Windows that Wine struggles with. The whole program is one small EXE that uses standard window controls and basic math libraries — exactly what Wine 1.7.55 implements well.

Boot Wine, upload your calc.exe, and you get the familiar grey calculator window. Switch between Standard and Scientific views from the View menu, copy and paste results, and use the keyboard or on-screen buttons. It all works as expected at near-instant speed, because there's almost nothing to emulate.

sections.h: What you can and can't run
sections.html:
Be aware there are two very different "Windows Calculators," and only one of them belongs here:

  • Classic calc.exe (Win 95 – Windows 7, also XP-era 5.1) — a native Win32 app. This is the one that runs well. Multiple Wine users confirm the XP/Win7-era classic calculator launches under Wine without fuss.
  • Modern "Calculator" (Windows 10/11) — a UWP app built with newer .NET and WinRT. Microsoft open-sourced its code under the MIT License in 2019, but it is not a Win32 EXE and will not run under Wine 1.7.55. Don't expect the tiled, full-screen Windows 10 calculator to work.

So: target the small, classic calc.exe. If you grab a modern Windows 10 machine's calc, you'll mostly find a tiny stub that just launches the UWP app — that stub won't do anything useful here.

sections.h: How to load it and get results out
sections.html:
A single EXE is all you need. Upload calc.exe on its own — there are no extra DLLs to bundle for the classic version. Pick the Win32 (default) variant, which is the everyday choice and the right one here.

The calculator is stateless, so there's nothing to save. If you do want to keep a result, copy it with Ctrl+C inside the app and paste it where you need it. Remember the virtual C:\ drive is wiped when you reload the tab — but for a calculator that doesn't matter, since there's nothing to persist.

faq.q: Is the Windows Calculator free to download here?
faq.a: No. The classic calc.exe is proprietary Microsoft software covered by your Windows license, so we don't host or distribute it. If you own a legal copy of Windows, you already have the file in C:\Windows\System32\ — copy it from there and upload it. The MIT-licensed version Microsoft released in 2019 is the modern UWP Calculator, which is a different app that won't run here.

faq.q: Does the classic calculator actually run under browser-based Wine?
faq.a: Yes, very reliably. It's a small, standard Win32 program with no GPU, 64-bit, .NET, or networking requirements, which is exactly the kind of app Wine 1.7.55 handles best. The XP and Windows 7 era calc.exe is well-documented as running under desktop Wine, and it behaves the same way here.

faq.q: Will the Windows 10 or Windows 11 Calculator work?
faq.a: No. The modern Calculator is a UWP app built on newer .NET and WinRT, not a Win32 EXE, so it won't run under Wine 1.7.55. On Windows 10/11 the file named calc.exe is usually just a stub that launches that UWP app. Use the older classic calculator (Windows 7 or earlier) instead.

faq.q: Where do I find calc.exe to upload?
faq.a: On a Windows machine you're licensed to use, look in C:\Windows\System32\ for calc.exe (Windows XP through 7) or win32calc.exe on some later builds. Copy that single file to your computer and upload it here. Microsoft also ships the classic calculator as an official licensed component for Windows IoT Enterprise. Please don't use cracked or dubious 'abandonware' downloads of Windows system files.

faq.q: Do I need a special Wine variant for the calculator?
faq.a: No — use the Win32 (default) variant. The classic calculator is a plain 32-bit Win32 app, so the everyday default runtime is the right choice. There's no need for the Gecko, Win 3.x, or r18 variants.

ogTitle: Character Map in Your Browser — Load Your Own charmap.exe (Guide)
ogDescription: The classic symbol-picker is a tiny Win32 utility that runs well in browser Wine — but you supply charmap.exe from your own Windows install, and Wine's font list is shorter.
h1: Running Character Map in your browser — with your own copy
author: Microsoft Corporation

verdict.text: Runs — but fewer fonts than on Windows

licenseReason: charmap.exe is a copyrighted Microsoft Windows component (all rights reserved), so it is not freely redistributable and we cannot host it.
licenseNote:
A licensing note

charmap.exe is part of Microsoft Windows and is Microsoft's copyrighted property — we can't host it, and you should only run a copy you already own. The simplest legitimate source is your own Windows installation: it lives at C:\Windows\System32\charmap.exe. Copy it from a PC you own, then load it here. Don't download "free charmap.exe" files from random sites — those are a common malware vector, and you don't need them. The free, fully-legal alternatives below are the easier route.
intro: The classic Windows Character Map (charmap.exe) — the little utility you open to find an em dash, a degree sign, an accented letter, or some obscure symbol and copy it to the clipboard. It's a tiny, single-purpose Win32 GUI program with no DirectX, no 3D, no .NET and no networking, which is exactly the kind of app browser-based Wine runs well — though since it's Microsoft's file we can't host it, you load your own copy below and it runs entirely in your browser tab. The honest catch: Character Map is only as useful as the fonts installed alongside it, and a fresh Wine environment ships far fewer fonts than real Windows — so it launches and works, but you'll see a shorter font list and fewer exotic glyphs than you would on a full Windows install.

sections.h: How it works & what to expect
sections.html:
charmap.exe is one of the lightest things you can run here — a single small executable with a standard window full of glyph cells, a font dropdown, a search box and a copy button. There's no graphics acceleration or modern framework involved, so it boots quickly and the interface behaves normally: pick a font, click a character, hit Select then Copy, and paste it into another app running in the same Wine session.

The big real-world limitation is fonts. Character Map doesn't contain any characters itself — it just displays whatever fonts are installed and lets you browse their glyphs. On real Windows you have dozens of fonts (Arial, Segoe UI, the big Unicode faces), so you can find almost any symbol. Inside browser-based Wine you only get Wine's bundled substitute fonts plus anything you add, so the dropdown is short and coverage of rare scripts and emoji is thin. Common Latin punctuation, accents and basic symbols are fine; deep Unicode is not.

AppWindows Character Map (charmap.exe)
Best Wine variantWin32 (default)
How to loadCopy charmap.exe from your own C:\Windows\System32 and upload it
What worksLaunches, browses installed fonts, copies glyphs to the clipboard
What's limitedFont list is short; rare scripts, CJK and emoji are mostly missing

sections.h: Better: free alternatives (and the no-app route)
sections.html:
Because charmap.exe can't be hosted and is font-limited under Wine, for most people there are quicker, fully-legal options:

  • Your OS already has one. Windows has Character Map built in; macOS has the Character Viewer (Ctrl+Cmd+Space); most Linux desktops include gnome-characters or KCharSelect. No browser needed.
  • Open-source pickers run cleanly here. Small GPL/MIT character-picker and Unicode utilities are freely redistributable and, being tiny Win32 apps, run well in ExeBrowser — and you're allowed to load them.
  • A plain web character picker on any normal web page needs no emulation at all and has the full Unicode set behind it.

If you specifically want the genuine Windows Character Map look-and-feel, copy charmap.exe from a PC you own and load it with the steps below.

1. On the home page, keep Win32 (default) and click Boot Wine.
  2. On a Windows PC you own, copy charmap.exe from C:\Windows\System32.
  3. Use the file/folder picker here to upload it (no extra DLLs are usually needed).
  4. Select the charmap.exe entry and click Run in Wine.
  5. Choose a font, click a character, press Select then Copy, and paste it into another window in the same session.

faq.q: Can I run Windows Character Map in the browser for free?
faq.a: You can run it, but you have to bring your own copy. charmap.exe is a copyrighted part of Windows, so we can't host it for you. Copy it from your own Windows PC (it's in C:\Windows\System32) and upload it — then it runs in the browser via Wine + WebAssembly with nothing to install.

faq.q: Why does Character Map show so few fonts here?
faq.a: Character Map only displays fonts that are actually installed. Real Windows ships dozens of fonts with huge Unicode coverage; a fresh browser-based Wine environment ships only a small set of substitute fonts. So the program runs fine, but the font dropdown is short and many rare symbols, CJK characters and emoji simply aren't present to browse.

faq.q: Is charmap.exe safe to download from a third-party site?
faq.a: No — don't. There's no legitimate standalone download of Character Map, and "free charmap.exe" files on random sites are a well-known malware lure. The only safe source is your own genuine Windows installation, where the file already exists in System32.

faq.q: Do I even need Character Map, or is there an easier way to get special characters?
faq.a: For most people there's an easier way. Your own operating system already has a character picker built in (Windows Character Map, the macOS Character Viewer, or GNOME/KDE tools on Linux), and ordinary web-based character pickers have the full Unicode set with no emulation at all. Running charmap.exe here is mainly for when you specifically want the genuine Windows utility.

faq.q: Will Character Map crash or need DirectX or .NET?
faq.a: No. Character Map is a plain Win32 GUI utility with no DirectX, no 3D and no .NET dependency, so it's one of the lighter things to run in ExeBrowser and starts quickly. Its only real limitation here is the smaller set of installed fonts, not stability.

title: Why KeePassXC Won't Run in a Browser — KeePass 1.x Does
description: KeePassXC is a 64-bit Qt5 app, so it can't load on ExeBrowser's 32-bit Wine 1.7.55. Here's why — and how KeePass 1.x Classic works in the browser instead.
keywords: keepassxc browser, run keepassxc online, keepassxc wine, keepassxc 32-bit, keepassxc webassembly, open source password manager browser, keepass classic browser, kdbx in browser
ogTitle: Why KeePassXC Won't Run in a Browser — And the KeePass 1.x That Does
ogDescription: KeePassXC targets 64-bit Windows with Qt5, which Boxedwine's 32-bit Wine can't run. This page explains the mismatch and points to KeePass 1.x Classic, which does work in a tab.
h1: Why KeePassXC won't run in a browser (and what does)
author: KeePassXC Team

verdict.text: Won't run — 64-bit Qt5 app

licenseReason: KeePassXC is licensed under GPL-2.0/GPL-3.0, so it is free and legal to redistribute — but it won't run on a 32-bit Wine 1.7.55 engine.
licenseNote:
Free software — but get it from the official source

KeePassXC is genuinely free and open source (GPL-2.0/GPL-3.0), so there's nothing to buy and nothing shady about it. To use it on a real machine, download the official build from keepassxc.org/download. Avoid third-party "free download" mirrors for a tool that guards your passwords — only the official site and verified package managers are trustworthy here.
intro: KeePassXC is a superb, modern, community-driven password manager — and we'd love to tell you it runs here. It doesn't. ExeBrowser uses Boxedwine (Wine 1.7.55 on a 32-bit x86 emulator), and KeePassXC is a 64-bit, Qt5 application that targets Windows 10/11. Those two facts don't meet in the middle. This page is the honest version: why KeePassXC can't load, and the open-source alternative — KeePass 1.x Classic — that actually does work in the browser.

sections.h: How it works & what to expect
sections.html:
Short answer: it won't start. There are two independent reasons, and either one alone is enough to stop it.

  • It's 64-bit only. KeePassXC 2.7.0 and newer ship as 64-bit Windows 10/11 builds exclusively. ExeBrowser's emulator is 32-bit x86 — a 64-bit executable simply cannot be loaded by it.
  • It's a heavy Qt5 app. The last build that ever shipped a 32-bit binary was 2.6.6, and even that is a large Qt5 application expecting Windows 7-or-later system libraries. Boxedwine's Wine 1.7.55 dates from around 2015 and emulates an older Windows environment; the modern Qt5 platform layer that KeePassXC needs to draw a single window isn't there.

So the realistic outcome is a crash or a blank window on launch — not a usable password manager. We set the verdict to Won't run rather than letting you waste time on it.

sections.h: What to use instead: KeePass 1.x Classic
sections.html:
Good news: the original KeePass has a native Win32 "Classic" line that does run under browser Wine. KeePass 1.x is a small, dependency-light Win32 program with no .NET and no Qt — exactly the kind of app Boxedwine handles well. It reads .kdb databases and gives you the core of what you want: open a vault, browse and copy entries, save changes.

Head to our KeePass in the browser guide for the step-by-step. The one caveat: KeePass 1.x uses the older .kdb format, which is different from KeePassXC's .kdbx. If your vault is .kdbx, you'd convert or export it on a real machine first.

sections.h: A serious word on password-vault safety
sections.html: Even when something does run here, think hard before opening a real password database in a browser tab. ExeBrowser runs everything locally and never uploads your files — your vault doesn't leave your machine — but a password store is the single most sensitive file you own. For day-to-day use, run a password manager natively on a trusted device. Treat in-browser Wine as an emergency way to view a vault on a computer where you can't install anything, not as your primary manager. Always close the tab when you're done; the in-memory drive is wiped on reload.

faq.q: Can I run KeePassXC in the browser with ExeBrowser?
faq.a: No. KeePassXC 2.7.0+ is a 64-bit Windows 10/11 application, and ExeBrowser's engine is 32-bit only. Even the last 32-bit build (2.6.6) is a Qt5 app that needs a modern Windows environment that Wine 1.7.55 doesn't provide. It will crash or show a blank window rather than open.

faq.q: Is KeePassXC free and safe to download?
faq.a: Yes. KeePassXC is free and open source under the GPL-2.0/GPL-3.0 license, with no purchase required. Always download it from the official site at keepassxc.org/download rather than third-party mirrors — it guards your passwords, so the source matters.

faq.q: What's the difference between KeePass and KeePassXC?
faq.a: KeePass is the original Windows project; KeePass 1.x is a native Win32 build and KeePass 2.x is .NET-based. KeePassXC is a separate cross-platform rewrite built on Qt. For running in the browser, only KeePass 1.x Classic works — see our KeePass guide.

faq.q: Which password manager actually works in ExeBrowser?
faq.a: KeePass 1.x (Classic) — the native Win32 edition with no .NET or Qt dependencies. It opens .kdb databases and runs under the default Win32 Wine variant. KeePass 2.x (.NET) and KeePassXC (64-bit Qt) do not run.

faq.q: Can I convert my KeePassXC .kdbx file to use in the browser?
faq.a: On a real machine, yes — KeePass and KeePassXC can import and export between the .kdbx and older .kdb formats. To view a vault in the browser you'd export it to .kdb for KeePass 1.x first, since KeePassXC itself won't run here.

ogTitle: Can You Run Dia in a Browser? Wine Guide (Free Visio Alternative)
ogDescription: Dia, the open-source GPL diagram and flowchart editor, loads in a browser tab if you supply your installed copy. Honest verdict: it runs, but the heavy GTK stack means a slow start.
h1: Can you run Dia Diagram Editor in your browser?
author: The Dia Developers (GNOME project)
licenseReason: Dia is released under the GNU GPL-2.0, an open-source license that explicitly permits free redistribution, so we can host the portable build.

verdict.text: Partial — loads, but heavy GTK app starts slowly

intro: Dia is a free, open-source diagram editor — the classic GPL alternative to Microsoft Visio — and this guide covers loading your own installed copy and running it in a browser tab. It draws flowcharts, network diagrams, UML, ER models, circuits, and more from a big palette of ready-made shapes. The Windows build is a 32-bit GTK+ application, which is good news for compatibility (no DirectX, no 64-bit, no modern .NET) but also a caveat: GTK apps drag a large stack of DLLs and image loaders behind them, so under browser-based Wine you should expect a slow first launch and somewhat sluggish redraws. Once it's up, basic diagramming generally works. Set this honestly: it runs, but it is not as snappy as a plain Win32 tool like Notepad.

sections.h: How it works & what to expect
sections.html:
Dia on Windows is built on the GTK+ 2.x toolkit. The portable build ships its own GTK runtime — dozens of DLLs plus the GDK-Pixbuf image loaders — all of which Boxedwine has to map and initialise before the main window appears. On native Windows that takes a moment; inside WebAssembly-emulated Wine at roughly 10-40% of native speed, the cold start can take noticeably longer, and the canvas may feel laggy when you drag shapes or scroll. Be patient on first boot and give it time to finish loading before you click around.

What works: opening the app, placing shapes from the toolbox, drawing connectors, typing labels, and saving a .dia file. What's rough: startup speed, large diagrams, and occasional quirks in GTK's file-chooser dialog. This is why we rate it partial rather than "works well" — it's genuinely usable for quick diagrams, not a polished daily driver.

sections.h: Loading Dia and saving your diagram
sections.html:
Dia is a folder of files, not a single self-contained EXE — it needs its bin\dia.exe plus the GTK lib/etc/share directories alongside it. Use the portable ZIP (below, or the official dia_0.97.2_win32.zip), unpack it, and upload the whole folder so Wine can find the runtime. Launch dia.exe and wait for the window to appear.

When you've drawn something, save it inside the app as a .dia file (or export to PNG/SVG via File → Export), then click Download files written by this app to pull your work out of the in-memory C:\ drive as a zip. The virtual drive is wiped when you reload the tab, so always download before you close it.

sections.h: Why use Dia in the browser at all
sections.html: The honest pitch: if you're on a Chromebook, a locked-down work laptop, or any machine where you can't install software, Dia-in-the-browser lets you sketch a flowchart or network diagram and export it as an image without touching the host OS. It opens and writes the open .dia XML format, and exports to PNG, SVG, and EPS. For a one-off diagram that's a real win. For heavy, day-in-day-out diagramming you'll have a better time installing Dia natively — but as a no-install, zero-upload-to-a-server option, it does the job.

faq.q: Is Dia free, and is it a good Visio alternative?
faq.a: Yes. Dia is free and open-source under the GNU GPL-2.0, and it's the long-standing open alternative to Microsoft Visio. It handles flowcharts, UML, network diagrams, ER models, and more from a large shape library. It's not a feature-for-feature Visio clone, but for most structured-diagram needs it's plenty.

faq.q: Does Dia actually run well in the browser?
faq.a: It runs, but expect a slow start. Dia is a GTK+ application with a large runtime, and Boxedwine emulates a 32-bit x86 CPU in WebAssembly at roughly 10-40% of native speed, so the first launch is slow and the canvas can feel laggy. Small, quick diagrams are fine; large or complex ones will test your patience. That's why we rate it partial, not 'works well'.

faq.q: Which Wine variant should I pick for Dia?
faq.a: Start with the default (Win32) variant — Dia is a standard 32-bit Windows app and doesn't need the bundled-Gecko or 16-bit modes. If the default build crashes on launch, try the r18 variant, which uses an older Boxedwine engine that sometimes handles finicky apps differently.

faq.q: How do I get my diagram out after I draw it?
faq.a: Save your work inside Dia as a .dia file, or use File → Export to write a PNG or SVG. Then click Download files written by this app to download everything the app wrote to the virtual C:\ drive as a zip. Do this before reloading or closing the tab, because the in-memory drive is erased on reload.

faq.q: Why is Dia slow to start in the browser?
faq.a: Because it's a GTK app. Before its window appears, Dia has to load dozens of GTK runtime DLLs and the GDK-Pixbuf image loaders. Even on native Windows GTK startup isn't instant, and under emulated Wine in WebAssembly that overhead is multiplied. Give it time on the first launch instead of clicking repeatedly.

download.heading: Download Dia (portable, GPL-2.0)
download.html:
Dia is open-source under the GPL-2.0, so you can fetch a portable Windows build and load the whole folder into ExeBrowser with "Load your own copy" above — the EXE needs its bundled GTK runtime beside it, then launch dia.exe.

Get the official Windows build and source from the Dia project on SourceForge (look for dia_0.97.2_win32.zip).

title: Why Inkscape Won't Run Well in a Browser — What to Use
description: Inkscape's heavy GTK+ and Cairo engine fights browser-based Wine — even classic 0.48–0.92 builds crash. Why the free SVG editor fails here, and what to try.
keywords: inkscape browser, run inkscape online, inkscape svg editor wine, free vector editor browser, inkscape classic 0.48 0.91 webassembly, open source vector graphics online
ogTitle: Why Inkscape Won't Run Well in a Browser — And What to Use Instead
ogDescription: Inkscape is free GPL software, but its heavy GTK+ engine is a hard target for browser-based Wine — expect slow starts, glitches, and crashes. Here's why, and better options.
h1: Why Inkscape (classic) doesn't run well in a browser
author: Inkscape Project

verdict.text: Heavy — GTK engine fights Wine, expect crashes

licenseReason: Inkscape is released under the GNU GPLv2, which freely permits redistribution, so it is legally hostable — but the classic Windows builds are very heavy to run here.
intro: Inkscape is the best-loved free, open-source vector graphics editor — a genuine alternative to Illustrator for drawing SVGs, logos, and illustrations. The license is great news (it is GPL, so it is free to download and share), but the engineering is the catch. Inkscape is built on the heavy GTK+ toolkit with Cairo rendering and a Python scripting layer, and that is a hard target for browser-based Wine. Be warned up front: even the classic 32-bit builds are slow to start, prone to rendering glitches, and frequently crash here. Treat this as an experiment, not a daily driver.

sections.html:
Modern Inkscape (1.0 and later) is 64-bit only and built on GTK+ 3, so it is a non-starter — ExeBrowser runs 32-bit Win32 only. Your only realistic candidates are the classic GTK+ 2 era builds: 0.48 (2010), 0.91 (2015), or the final GTK2 release 0.92.x (2017), all of which shipped 32-bit Windows installers. These are the lightest Inkscape has ever been on Windows, which is exactly why they are the ones worth trying.

AppInkscape classic, 32-bit (inkscape.exe)
LicenseGNU GPLv2 — free and open source
Best Wine variantWin32 (default); try r18 if default crashes on launch
EngineGTK+ 2.x toolkit + Cairo rendering + Python extensions
Where to get itinkscape.org — 32-bit Windows archive (official)

Inkscape leans on almost everything Wine 1.7.55 finds difficult at once. The GTK+ widget set is large and draws through Cairo, which means a lot of software-rendered redraws on every pan, zoom, and dialog — painful at the ~10–40% of native speed Boxedwine delivers. The multi-window, dockable-panel interface stresses the parts of Wine that are weakest in this emulator, and the bundled Python interpreter (used for extensions and many menu actions) often fails to initialize. The practical result is long startup times, blank or half-drawn panels, sluggish canvas redraws, and a real chance the app never reaches a usable window at all.

sections.h: How to load it if you want to try anyway
sections.html: Inkscape ships as an installer (and modern ones as an MSI), which will not run well here directly. Install a classic 32-bit build on a real Windows PC, then upload the whole resulting Inkscape program folder — inkscape.exe plus its lib\, etc\, share\, and python\ subfolders — using the folder picker. Do not upload just the EXE; without its GTK and theme files it cannot start. Give it time on first launch, and if it crashes immediately on the default engine, reload and try the r18 variant. If you do get a drawing open, save inside the app and use Download files written by this app before you close the tab — the virtual C:\ is wiped on reload.

If you actually need to view or lightly edit an SVG in the browser, you have far better options than fighting Inkscape under Wine. SVG is just XML, so for quick viewing or hand-editing nothing beats opening the file in a normal browser tab or a text editor. For real vector work on a locked-down machine, Inkscape itself runs natively and fast on Linux, macOS, and Windows — installing it directly will always beat emulating it. Within ExeBrowser, lighter open-source creative tools like the paint programs in our guide are much more dependable than a full GTK suite.

faq.q: Does Inkscape work in the browser on ExeBrowser?
faq.a: Not well. Inkscape is GPL open-source so it is legal to run, and the classic 32-bit 0.48–0.92 builds are the only ones that even have a chance under 32-bit Wine. In practice they are slow to start and crash-prone because of Inkscape's heavy GTK+/Cairo engine and Python layer. Consider it an experiment, not a working tool.

faq.q: Why can't I run the latest Inkscape (1.x or newer)?
faq.a: Modern Inkscape is 64-bit only and built on GTK+ 3. ExeBrowser runs 32-bit Win32 software only via Boxedwine, so 1.0+ will not load at all. The newest version you could even attempt is the GTK+ 2-based 0.92.x line from 2017.

faq.q: Is Inkscape free and legal to use?
faq.a: Yes. Inkscape is released under the GNU General Public License (GPLv2), which makes it free to download, use, and redistribute. There is nothing license-wise stopping you from running it; the limitation here is purely technical performance under emulation.

faq.q: What's the best free vector editor I can actually use right now?
faq.a: If you just need to view or tweak an SVG, open it in a regular browser tab or text editor — SVG is XML. For real drawing, install Inkscape natively on Linux, macOS, or Windows where it runs full speed. Browser-based Wine is the wrong tool for a heavyweight GTK app like this.

faq.q: It crashes on startup — is there anything I can try?
faq.a: Upload the complete program folder (not just inkscape.exe — it needs its lib, etc, share and python folders), give it extra time on first launch, and if the default engine crashes immediately, reload and switch to the r18 Wine variant. Even with all that, success is not guaranteed.

title: Why Blender Doesn't Run in a Browser — What to Do
description: Classic Blender (2.49b) won't work in browser Wine: its OpenGL-drawn UI has no hardware 3D under WebAssembly. Why it fails and what to use instead.
keywords: run blender in browser, blender online no download, blender wine webassembly, blender 2.49b portable, classic blender browser, blender opengl wine not working, blender free open source
ogTitle: Why Blender Doesn't Run in a Browser — And What to Do Instead
ogDescription: Blender's entire interface is drawn with OpenGL, and ExeBrowser's Wine + WebAssembly runtime has no hardware 3D acceleration — even classic 2.49b fails. Here's why, and the realistic ways to use Blender.
h1: Why Blender doesn't run in a browser (and what to use instead)
author: Blender Foundation

verdict.text: Won't work — 3D viewport needs OpenGL

licenseReason: Blender is free and open source under the GNU GPL, so it is fully legal to redistribute — but it still cannot render its 3D viewport without hardware OpenGL, which the browser runtime does not provide.
intro: Blender is the legendary free, open-source 3D suite — modeling, animation, rendering, the works. It is GPL-licensed, so there is no legal problem running or sharing it. The problem is technical, and we'd rather be straight with you: Blender's entire interface is drawn with OpenGL, and ExeBrowser's runtime (Boxedwine = Wine 1.7.55 + a 32-bit x86 CPU emulated in WebAssembly) has no hardware 3D acceleration. Even the oldest "classic" builds like 2.49b expect a real OpenGL surface to draw their viewport and menus. So while the blender.exe process may start, you should expect a black or garbled window, a crash on launch, or a UI you can't actually use. This page exists so you don't waste twenty minutes finding that out the hard way — and so you know the realistic options instead.

download.heading: Get Blender (free & open source)
download.html:
Always download Blender from the official source

Blender is genuinely free software (GNU GPL), so there's nothing to buy and nothing shady about it. Get it straight from the Blender Foundation — that's the safe, malware-free, always-current source:

Download Blender from blender.org →

Older “classic” releases (2.49b, 2.79, etc.) are preserved in the official archive at download.blender.org/release. These run beautifully natively on Windows, macOS and Linux. We're being upfront: even these older 32-bit builds need real hardware OpenGL, so they will not render usefully inside the browser runtime — install Blender on your actual desktop to use it.

sections.h: How it works & what to expect
sections.html:
ExeBrowser doesn't simulate Blender — it runs the real blender.exe through Wine on top of an x86 CPU emulated in WebAssembly. That part is faithful. What's missing is the graphics path.

Blender is not a normal “windows and buttons” app that draws with the standard Windows GDI. Every pixel of Blender's interface — the 3D viewport, the menus, the panels — is rendered through OpenGL, talking to your graphics card. Boxedwine provides no GPU and no accelerated OpenGL, so Blender has nothing to draw on. Realistically you'll see one of these:

  • Immediate crash / exit when Blender tries to create its OpenGL context.
  • A black or scrambled window with no usable interface.
  • At best, a frozen splash that never reaches a working viewport.

This is not a bug we can fix on a single page — it's a fundamental limit of running a GPU-driven 3D app on a software-only, no-OpenGL runtime. Set your expectations to “this is a curiosity, not a workflow.”

sections.h: Why even classic Blender (2.49b) won't render here
sections.html:
People reasonably assume the old versions are lighter and might squeak by. They are lighter on CPU and RAM, and they are real 32-bit Win32 executables — which is exactly what this runtime targets. But the blocker isn't CPU or memory; it's the graphics API.

Blender has required OpenGL for its viewport since its earliest public releases. Modern Blender demands OpenGL 3.3+, and even 2.49b-era builds need a working OpenGL driver to draw anything at all. The browser runtime has no OpenGL acceleration of any kind, so there is no version of Blender — old or new — that gets a usable viewport here. Choosing an older build doesn't route around the problem; the problem is the missing GPU layer.

sections.h: The realistic way to run Blender
sections.html:
Blender is free and runs superbly on real hardware. If you actually want to use it:

  1. Install it natively. blender.org/download has builds for Windows, macOS and Linux. This is the right answer for 99% of people.
  2. Need an old release? Grab 2.49b, 2.79 or any historical version from the official release archive and run it on your desktop.
  3. On a locked-down machine? A desktop Wine install or a real virtual machine with GPU/OpenGL passthrough can run Blender — the browser sandbox cannot, because it has no GPU access to pass through.

If what you actually want is a browser-based 3D tool, look for apps built for the web (WebGL-native editors) rather than a Windows .exe pushed through an emulator. ExeBrowser shines with 2D apps, retro games and utilities — not GPU-bound 3D suites.

faq.q: Can I run Blender online in the browser with no download?
faq.a: Not usefully. The real blender.exe can start under our Wine + WebAssembly runtime, but Blender draws its entire interface with OpenGL and the browser runtime has no hardware 3D acceleration. Expect a black/garbled window or a crash on launch rather than a working 3D viewport.

faq.q: Is Blender free and legal to use?
faq.a: Yes. Blender is free and open source under the GNU General Public License (GPL). You can use, copy and redistribute it freely. There's no purchase, no trial and no piracy concern — just download it from blender.org.

faq.q: Will an old version like Blender 2.49b work in the browser?
faq.a: No. Older 32-bit builds are lighter on CPU and RAM, but the blocker is graphics, not horsepower. Every Blender version needs a working OpenGL driver to draw its viewport, and the browser runtime provides none. Choosing an old build doesn't get around the missing GPU layer.

faq.q: Why does Blender need OpenGL when other apps run fine here?
faq.a: Most apps that work in ExeBrowser draw with the standard Windows GDI (plain windows, text and buttons), which the runtime emulates in software. Blender renders its whole UI and 3D viewport through OpenGL, talking directly to a graphics card — and there's no GPU in the browser sandbox to talk to.

faq.q: What should I use instead to run Blender?
faq.a: Install Blender natively on Windows, macOS or Linux from blender.org/download — it's free and runs great. Need a historical release? The official archive has every old version. A real VM with GPU passthrough also works; the browser cannot, because it has no GPU to pass through.

intro:
Cosmo's Cosmic Adventure — Apogee's 1992 platformer, in which a small green alien crash-lands on an unknown planet while looking for his parents and has to climb his way out using nothing but his own suction-cup hands. The complete shareware Episode 1, "Forbidden Planet", is hosted here: click Play and the original DOS game boots in your browser via DOSBox + WebAssembly.

It's remembered for one genuinely clever mechanic — Cosmo can't shoot, so climbing walls and dropping bombs is your entire toolkit, and the level design is built around that constraint.

sections.h: How it works & what to expect
sections.html: This is the original 1992 DOS release running in a WebAssembly build of DOSBox. The package is tiny (under 500 KB), so it boots almost instantly. Cosmo's suction hands grab any wall you jump into — hold the direction to cling, then climb. Bombs are limited and mainly for clearing blocked routes rather than enemies.

Jumping onto an enemy's head is your main attack, and bouncing off one gains you extra height — several routes need that. Cling to a wall and wait when something is patrolling below; patience beats speed in most rooms. The green bars in the HUD are health, and stars are the score pickups worth detouring for.

sections.h: Shareware episode — and the full trilogy
sections.html: Episode 1 is the complete free shareware episode Apogee distributed. Episodes 2 and 3 were the commercial purchase, and the trilogy is still sold — you'll find it on Steam and GOG as Cosmo's Cosmic Adventure. If you enjoy the episode, buying the full set supports the rights holder.

intro: Duke Nukem 3D — 3D Realms' 1996 Build-engine shooter, the one with the pig cops, the interactive everything and the one-liners. The shareware episode, L.A. Meltdown, is hosted here exactly as 3D Realms released it — click Play and it boots in your browser. Leave it alone at the title screen and it plays its own demo; press Esc for the menu and pick New Game.

sections.h: How it works & what to expect
sections.html: The original DOS release (version 1.3D) running in a WebAssembly build of DOSBox, set to give it as much CPU as your device has. On a recent laptop or desktop it plays smoothly; a phone or an older Chromebook will be choppier, because every instruction of a game that wanted a fast 486 is being emulated. The package is under 6 MB and is cached after the first load.

Keys open doors and the coloured card readers — the shareware levels hide them behind vents you can kick or shoot open. Hold Shift to run, which you will want almost all the time. The jetpack and steroids in your inventory are selected with [ and ] and used with Enter. Mirrors, toilets and arcade cabinets all react — that is the game, not a bug.

sections.h: Shareware episode — and the full game
sections.html: Episode 1 is the shareware episode, and its licence lets free websites offer it — so long as every one of its files ships unmodified, which they do here. Episodes 2 and 3 (and the later Atomic Edition's fourth) were the commercial release and are not included; the full game is still sold.

faq.q: Is Duke Nukem 3D legal to play here?
faq.a: Yes. This is the official shareware episode, whose licence explicitly allows free websites to make it available. The commercial episodes are not hosted.

faq.q: What are the controls?
faq.a: Arrow keys move, Ctrl fires, Space opens doors and uses switches, A jumps, Z crouches, Shift runs and Tab shows the map. The full table is under the game.

faq.q: Why is it slow on my phone?
faq.a: Duke 3D wanted a fast 486 in 1996, and here every one of its instructions is emulated in your browser. A recent desktop or laptop handles it; a phone or a budget Chromebook will drop frames.

faq.q: Does my progress save?
faq.a: Yes — saved games persist in this browser between visits, best-effort. Save from the game's own menu with F2.

faq.q: Can I play the full game here?
faq.a: Only the shareware episode is hosted. If you own the DOS version, drop its folder into the DOS emulator page and it runs the same way.

intro: Dune II: The Building of a Dynasty — Westwood's 1992 game, and the template for every real-time strategy game since. Choose House Atreides, Harkonnen or Ordos, harvest spice to fund a base, and build an army to drive the other Houses off Arrakis while sandworms swallow anything left on open sand. The intro takes a while to load; press Esc to skip it.

sections.html: Dune II introduced the building blocks of the genre: resource harvesting, a build tree that opens as you construct buildings, a fog of war over an unexplored map, and units that fight in real time. Westwood built Command & Conquer on the same design three years later. Units are ordered one at a time, which was standard in 1992; select a unit, click an order such as Move or Attack, then click the target.

Build a second Spice Refinery and a couple of harvesters early; credits limit everything else. Concrete slabs under buildings stop them crumbling. Keep harvesters off open sand when a worm sign appears.

intro: Sudoku is the number-placement puzzle in which every row, column and block of a 9×9 grid holds each digit from 1 to 9 exactly once. This version generates a fresh grid every time, at the difficulty you pick, and includes Jigsaw, Killer and X variants. The puzzle is ready below; click a square and type a digit to start.

sections.html:
Fill every empty square with a digit so that:

  • no digit repeats in any row;
  • no digit repeats in any column;
  • no digit repeats in any block outlined by thick lines.

Some squares are filled in for you as clues. In X mode the two long diagonals (shaded) must also contain each digit once. In Killer mode there are no starting digits; instead, dashed cages show the total their digits must add up to, and no digit may repeat inside a cage. Larger grids run out of digits, so they use letters after 9 (a 12×12 grid uses 1–9 then a, b, c).

The Type menu offers 2×2 (a 4×4 grid), 2×3 (a 6×6 grid), the standard 3×3 (9×9) and larger 3×4 and 4×4 grids. Difficulty runs Trivial, Basic, Intermediate, Advanced, Extreme and Unreasonable: up to Basic there is always at least one square you can fill outright, Intermediate and above need deductions about where a digit could go, and Unreasonable may need trial and error. There are also presets for X mode, Killer mode and 9-square Jigsaw grids with irregular blocks. Hard settings can take a few seconds to generate.

Start with the digit that is already placed most often and check each block for the single square it can go in. When a block's options for a digit all lie in one row or column, that digit is ruled out of the rest of that row or column. Use pencil marks once single placements dry up: two squares in a unit that can only hold the same two digits (a naked pair) let you strike those digits from everywhere else in the unit. In Killer, learn the forced combinations, for example a two-square cage totalling 3 must be 1 and 2.

Solo is part of Simon Tatham's Portable Puzzle Collection, a set of about forty logic puzzles written by Simon Tatham and contributors and released under the MIT licence. Every grid is generated on the spot, so the supply never runs out, and for the grid-logic puzzles the generator makes sure each has exactly one solution, reachable by reasoning rather than guessing. The version here is the collection's own code compiled to WebAssembly; the Game menu can save a puzzle to a file and load it again, and the Type menu changes the size and difficulty.

faq.q: Does every puzzle have exactly one solution?
faq.a: Yes. The generator only offers grids that can be solved by logic to a single answer; at the Unreasonable level you may need to try a digit and backtrack, but the answer is still unique.

faq.q: Can I type in a Sudoku from a newspaper?
faq.a: Yes. Use Game → Specific to enter a puzzle description, and the built-in solver can also solve grids it did not generate itself.

faq.q: Is Sudoku free to play here?
faq.a: Yes, with no limit on the number of puzzles. Solo is open-source software under the MIT licence, and every grid is generated fresh when you press New game.

faq.q: Does it work on a phone or tablet?
faq.a: Yes. A tap works as a click and the puzzle resizes to fit the screen. Puzzles whose controls use the right mouse button are easier with a mouse.

intro: A nonogram (also called paint-by-numbers or Hanjie) is a grid you shade black and white using the numbers beside each row and above each column. Each number is the length of a run of black squares, in order. This version generates new grids endlessly. The puzzle is ready below; left-click a square to shade it black.

sections.html:
• Every square ends up either black or white.
  • The numbers beside a row give the lengths of its black runs, from left to right; the numbers above a column give its runs from top to bottom.
  • Runs in the same line are separated by at least one white square.

Because the grids are generated rather than drawn, the finished result is a random pattern rather than a picture, so you cannot guess squares from the image; every square has to be worked out.
The Type menu offers square grids of 10×10, 15×15, 20×20, 25×25 and 30×30. Bigger grids are not harder rule-wise but take much longer. Custom lets you set any width and height.

Look for long runs first: if a run is longer than half the line, the squares where every possible position overlaps must be black. Add up the clues plus one gap between each run; if that total equals the line length, the line is fully determined. Mark known whites as you go, since they split a line into shorter sections and create new overlaps. Work back and forth between rows and columns, revisiting any line that a new square has touched.

intro: Calcudoku combines a Latin square with arithmetic: every row and column holds each number once, and outlined cages show a target and an operation (add, subtract, multiply or divide) their digits must produce. It is widely published under the name KenKen. The puzzle is ready below; click a square and type a digit to begin.

sections.html:
On an N×N grid, fill each square with a digit from 1 to N so that:

  • each digit appears once in every row and once in every column;
  • the digits in each cage, combined with the cage's operation, give its target number.

A + cage is a sum and a × cage is a product. A − or ÷ cage always covers two squares; the larger digit minus (or divided by) the smaller gives the target, in either order. A digit may repeat inside a cage, as long as the repeats are not in the same row or column.

Presets run from 4×4 Easy up to 9×9 Normal, with 6×6 offered at Easy, Normal, Hard, Extreme and Unreasonable. Unreasonable may need trial and error; the levels below it can all be solved by reasoning alone. Some presets are "multiplication only", where every cage is a product (a variant sometimes called Inshi no Heya).

Fill single-square cages first: their target is the digit. Two-square cages with large products narrow quickly, so 12× on a 4×4 grid must be 3 and 4. Use the row and column totals: every row of an N×N grid adds up to the same amount, so a nearly complete row can tell you what a straddling cage must contribute. Pencil in candidates (M fills them all) and strike out those that clash with a row or column.

Keen is part of Simon Tatham's Portable Puzzle Collection, a set of about forty logic puzzles written by Simon Tatham and contributors and released under the MIT licence. Every grid is generated on the spot, so the supply never runs out, and for the grid-logic puzzles the generator makes sure each has exactly one solution, reachable by reasoning rather than guessing. sections.html:
On an N×N grid, build a tower in each square with a height from 1 to N so that:

  • each height appears once in every row and once in every column;
  • each edge clue equals the number of towers visible from that point, looking along the row or column; a tower is hidden if any taller tower stands in front of it.

So a clue of N means the heights rise steadily away from it, and a clue of 1 means the tallest tower is right next to it. In larger or harder puzzles some towers are placed for you and some edge clues are missing.

Presets cover 4×4 Easy, 5×5 Easy and Hard, and 6×6 at Easy, Hard, Extreme and Unreasonable. Unreasonable needs some trial and error; the other levels can be reasoned out. Custom goes from 3×3 up to 9×9. If you find the 3D drawing hard to read, Preferences can switch to a flat 2D view with plain numbers.

Place the certainties first: a clue of 1 puts the tallest tower beside it, and a clue of N fixes the whole line in rising order. A tower of height N can never be closer to a clue than (clue − 1) squares away, so a clue of 3 keeps the tallest tower out of the first two squares. Opposite clues that add up to N+1 often pin the tallest tower's position exactly.

intro: Guess is a code-breaking game. The computer picks a hidden row of four coloured pegs from six colours, and you have ten tries to find it. After each guess, small marker pegs say how many of your pegs are the right colour in the right place, and how many are the right colour in the wrong place. sections.html:
• The hidden code is a row of coloured pegs; by default four pegs from six colours, and colours may repeat.
  • After each guess you get one black marker for each peg of the right colour in the right position.
  • You get one white marker for each peg of a right colour that is in the wrong position.
  • Find the code before your guesses run out (ten by default).

The Type menu has Standard (6 colours, 4 pegs, 10 guesses) and Super (8 colours, 5 pegs, 12 guesses). Custom sets the number of colours (2 to 10), pegs per guess and guesses, and whether repeated colours are allowed in the code (on by default) and whether you may use blank pegs in guesses (off by default, and they make it easier).

Open with guesses that test several colours at once, such as two pegs each of two colours, then use the feedback to narrow things down. Black and white counts together tell you how many of your colours appear at all, which is a good way to sort out the palette. Use hold markers to carry pegs you are sure of into the next row. Every new guess should be consistent with all the feedback so far.

Guess is part of Simon Tatham's Portable Puzzle Collection, a set of about forty logic puzzles written by Simon Tatham and contributors and released under the MIT licence. Every grid is generated on the spot, so the supply never runs out, and for the grid-logic puzzles the generator makes sure each has exactly one solution, reachable by reasoning rather than guessing. The version here is the collection's own code compiled to WebAssembly; the Game menu can save a puzzle to a file and load it again, and the Type menu changes the size and difficulty.

faq.q: Does it work on a phone or tablet?

intro: A chess board and an opponent that never gets tired of you. The computer is Stockfish 19, the strongest open-source chess engine there is, compiled to WebAssembly and running inside this page. You choose how hard it plays: level 1 picks loose moves and looks only one move ahead, level 8 thinks for a second and a half at full strength. Drag a piece or tap it and then a square; the board shows where it can go.

sections.html:
The eight levels combine Stockfish's own Skill Level setting, which makes it deliberately choose weaker moves, with a cap on how far ahead it searches. Roughly:

  • 1–2 — for learning the moves. It leaves pieces hanging and misses simple captures.
  • 3–4 — casual play. It punishes blunders but makes some of its own.
  • 5–6 — a good club player. Expect to lose material if you leave a tactic on the board.
  • 7–8 — very strong. Level 8 is full Stockfish with a short think; a draw against it is an achievement.

You can change the level mid-game; the next computer move uses the new setting.

Pick White, Black or Random and press New game. All the rules are enforced: castling, en passant, promotion (a picker offers queen, rook, bishop or knight), and every draw — stalemate, threefold repetition, the fifty-move rule and insufficient material. Undo takes back your last move and the computer's reply. The move list beside the board uses standard algebraic notation, so you can copy a game into any analysis tool afterwards.

If you close the tab mid-game, the position is kept in this browser and comes back next time you open the page.

Nothing is sent to a server. The engine is the single-threaded "lite" WebAssembly build of Stockfish 19 from the stockfish.js project, about 1.8 MB including its neural-network evaluation, and it runs in a background worker so the board stays responsive while it thinks. The board itself is chessground, the open-source board that lichess.org uses, and the rules come from chess.js. Because both Stockfish and chessground are GPL-licensed, the code of this page is released under the GPL too; it is served unminified at /apps/chess/.

faq.q: How strong is the computer at the highest level?
faq.a: Level 8 is Stockfish 19 at full strength with about 1.5 seconds per move. The lite network is a little weaker than desktop Stockfish, but it still plays far above any human. Lower levels are deliberately weakened with Stockfish's Skill Level option and a shallow search.

faq.q: Do I need an account?
faq.a: No. There is no sign-up and nothing is uploaded; the engine runs in your browser. Your unfinished game is saved in this browser's local storage.

faq.q: Can I play on my phone?
faq.a: Yes. Tap a piece and then the square you want; the board resizes to the screen. The engine is single-threaded, so it works on any modern phone browser without special settings.

faq.q: Can I play against a friend?
faq.a: Not on this page yet — it is one player against the computer. You can choose either colour and switch sides between games.

intro: Each puzzle starts from a real game at the moment one side made a mistake. The opponent's move is played for you; then it's your turn to find the move that punishes it — a fork, a pin, a mate, a winning exchange. Get it right and the opponent replies, and you keep going until the combination is complete. The puzzles come from the Lichess puzzle database, which its authors release into the public domain, and each one has been played and rated by thousands of people.

sections.html:
You start at 1200. Every puzzle has its own rating, and the next one is chosen close to yours. Solve a puzzle on the first try, without a hint, and your rating goes up — more for a puzzle rated above you, less for one below. A wrong move, a hint or Show solution counts as a miss and lowers it. It's the same Elo arithmetic chess ratings use, so after twenty or thirty puzzles the number settles around where you really are.

Your rating, streak and the puzzles you've already seen are stored in this browser only.

About 4,600 puzzles, 220 in every hundred-point band from 600 to 2700, chosen for being popular, well-tested and stable in rating. The themes shown under the board — mate in 2, fork, pin, discovered attack, back-rank mate and so on — come from the database's own tagging, so you can see what kind of idea you're looking for once you've found it. Each puzzle links back to its page on lichess.org if you want to see the game it came from.

Check every capture and every check first — most tactics start with one of them. Look for undefended pieces and for pieces that are defending two things at once. In a mate puzzle, any move that delivers checkmate counts, even if it isn't the one in the database.

faq.q: Where do the puzzles come from?
faq.a: From the Lichess puzzle database, which is published under CC0 (public domain). We host a selection of about 4,600 of its six million puzzles, spread evenly across the rating range.

faq.q: Why did my rating go down when I used a hint?
faq.a: A hint, a wrong move or Show solution counts as not solving the puzzle unaided, so the rating treats it as a miss. You can still finish the puzzle afterwards.

faq.q: Will I see the same puzzle twice?
faq.a: Not until you have worked through the puzzles near your rating; the page remembers the last 1,500 you've seen in this browser.

verdict.text: ▶ Play now — runs natively, no emulator

intro: The tile-matching patience game, played with a full set of 136 mahjong tiles stacked into a layout. Take tiles off in matching pairs; a tile can only be taken when nothing sits on top of it and it is open on its left or right side. Clear the whole stack to win. Unlike many versions, every deal here can be cleared: the tiles are laid out by playing a random game backwards, so a solution always exists — the challenge is finding it.

sections.html: Click a free tile, then another free tile with the same face, and both disappear. Blocked tiles are shaded darker. Identical faces match: the same number of the same suit (circles, bamboo or characters), the same wind or the same dragon. The counter above the board shows how many pairs are left and how many matches are open to you right now. When that number reaches zero you're stuck — press Undo to back out of the dead end, or Shuffle to rearrange the tiles still on the board.

• Turtle — the traditional shape: a wide base with stepped layers in the middle. The best place to start.
  • Pyramid — four layers rising to a small peak. The tiles you need are often buried deep, so open the top early.
  • Bridge — long and low, with two layers stacked on the centre span. Many tiles are blocked side-to-side rather than from above.
  • Fortress — a walled square with towers at the corners. The towers have to come down before the walls open up.

Prefer matches that free other tiles: a tile on top of a stack or at the end of a long row unlocks more than one in the open. When three or four of a face are free, think before you take two — the pair you leave behind may be the only way into a stack later. Hint shows one possible match, but not necessarily the best one. Shuffle keeps the game winnable, but undo history is cleared when you use it.

The game is our own code. The tile artwork is FluffyStuff's riichi mahjong tile set, which its author has dedicated to the public domain. That set has no flower or season tiles, so the layouts here use the 136 standard tiles — 34 faces, four of each — instead of the 144 some versions use.

faq.q: Is every game really winnable?
faq.a: Yes. Tiles are assigned by simulating a complete game in reverse — repeatedly picking two positions that would both be free and giving them the same face — so at least one way to clear the board exists. Shuffle uses the same method on the remaining tiles.

faq.q: Which tiles can I take?
faq.a: A tile is free when no tile lies on top of it (even partly) and at least one of its long sides — left or right — has no neighbour at the same height.

faq.q: Does it save my game?
faq.a: Yes. If you close the page mid-game, the layout and the tiles you've removed are kept in this browser and come back next time.

intro: Checkers by the American rules (English draughts) against a computer opponent. You play red and move first. Tap a piece and the squares it can reach light up; if a capture is available you must take it, and the board only lets you pick pieces that can. When a jump lands where another jump is possible, keep tapping landing squares until the move is complete.

sections.html:
• Pieces move one square diagonally forward, on the dark squares only.
  • Captures are compulsory: jump an adjacent enemy piece into the empty square behind it. If the landing square offers another jump, the same piece must continue.
  • A piece that reaches the far row is crowned king (marked ♛) and may then move and jump backwards too. Being crowned ends the move.
  • You lose when you have no legal move — usually because every piece is gone or blocked. Fifty moves each without a capture or a crowning is a draw.

Easy looks two moves ahead and plays loosely; Medium searches four; Hard searches seven and follows forced capture sequences to the end, so it won't walk into a trade it can't see. It values material, kings, advancement, the centre and keeping its back row home to stop you crowning.

Keep your back row intact for as long as you can — it's the cheapest defence against enemy kings. Trade pieces when you're ahead and avoid trades when behind. Because captures are forced, you can offer a piece to drag an opponent's man into a square where you get two back.

faq.q: Are captures forced?
faq.a: Yes, as in American checkers. If any jump is available you must take one, and a piece that can keep jumping must do so.

faq.q: Can kings fly across the board?
faq.a: No — these are American/English rules, where a king moves one square at a time in any diagonal direction. Flying kings belong to international and Russian draughts.

faq.q: Is my game saved?
faq.a: Yes, an unfinished game is kept in this browser and resumes when you come back.
