intro: Reversi is played on an 8×8 board with discs that are black on one side and white on the other. You play black and move first. Place a disc so that one or more straight lines of white discs are trapped between it and another black disc, and every trapped disc flips to black. Legal squares are marked with a dot. When the board fills — or neither side can move — whoever has more discs wins.

sections.html:
• The game starts with four discs in the centre, two of each colour on a diagonal.
  • Every move must flip at least one opposing disc, along a row, column or diagonal. A single move can flip lines in several directions at once.
  • If you have no legal move you pass; if neither side can move, the game ends.
  • The player with more discs at the end wins.

The game is also widely known by a trademarked name; the rules are the same.

Corners can never be flipped, so they are the most valuable squares on the board; the squares diagonally next to them are the most dangerous, because playing there usually hands the corner to your opponent. Early in the game, having fewer discs is often better — it leaves your opponent with fewer moves. Count disc totals only near the end. The computer plays exactly this way: corner-first square weights, mobility, and raw disc count once fewer than fourteen squares remain.

faq.q: Who moves first?
faq.a: Black moves first, and you play black.

faq.q: What happens if I have no legal move?
faq.a: You pass automatically and the computer moves again. If neither side can move, the game ends and the discs are counted.

faq.q: How strong is Hard?
faq.a: Hard searches five moves ahead with alpha-beta pruning and a positional evaluation. It is a solid club-level opponent but not a perfect player.

h1: Play backgammon against the computer
author: ExeBrowser (original implementation)

verdict.text: ▶ Play now — runs natively, no emulator

intro: Backgammon is a race with collisions. You and the computer each have fifteen checkers moving in opposite directions around the board; you move yours from the 24-point down to your home board (points 1–6) and bear them off. Land on a point held by a single enemy checker and you send it to the bar, where it must start again. First to bear off all fifteen wins. Press Roll, then tap a checker and a highlighted point for each die.

sections.html:
• Each die is a separate move: a 5 and a 3 move one checker eight points or two checkers five and three. Doubles are played four times.
  • You may not land on a point held by two or more enemy checkers.
  • A checker on the bar must re-enter in the opponent's home board before anything else moves.
  • You must use both dice if any legal sequence allows it; if only one can be used, it must be the larger when either would do. The board only offers moves that obey this.
  • Once all fifteen checkers are home you bear off, using a die equal to a checker's point, or a higher die on your highest checker.

A win is worth one point. If the loser hasn't borne off a single checker, it's a gammon and counts two; if the loser also still has a checker on the bar or in the winner's home board, it's a backgammon and counts three. The score carries over from game to game. There is no doubling cube in this version.

Make points rather than leaving single checkers (blots) where they can be hit — especially your 5-point and the bar point (7). A row of consecutive made points, a prime, can trap enemy checkers behind it. When you're well ahead in the race, stop fighting and run home. The pip counts above the board show how far each side has to go.

faq.q: Is the doubling cube included?
faq.a: Not yet. Games are scored as single wins, gammons and backgammons, with the score kept across games.

faq.q: Does the computer cheat with the dice?
faq.a: No. Both sides' dice come from the browser's random number generator, and the computer sees nothing you don't.

faq.q: How do I bear off?
faq.a: Once all fifteen of your checkers are on points 1–6, tap a checker and then the tray on the right edge of the board.

verdict.text: ▶ Play now — the real NetHack 3.6.7

intro: NetHack is the dungeon crawl that has been in development since 1987: descend through randomly generated levels, find the Amulet of Yendor at the bottom, and bring it back up — if you survive. This is the official NetHack 3.6.7 source compiled to WebAssembly, not a remake, so every interaction the game is famous for is here. Choose a name and a role, press Start, and click the game to give it the keyboard.

sections.html: Move with h j k l and y u b n for diagonals, or with the arrow keys and the numeric keypad. A capital letter (or Shift+arrow) runs. Some essentials: , pick up, i inventory, e eat, q quaff, r read, w wield, W wear, s search, < and > stairs, # extended commands such as #pray, ? help. Alt+letter sends NetHack's Meta commands. Click a spot on the map to travel there. On a phone, a keypad appears under the map with directions and the common keys, and ⌨ opens the system keyboard.

Press S and answer y to save and stop. The save is kept in this browser's storage; next time you open this page with the same name, the start button says Continue saved game and you pick up where you left off. As in NetHack itself there is no autosave — but if you close the tab without saving, the last save you made is still there, so you lose only the time since then.

Valkyrie is the most forgiving role for a first game: strong, cold-resistant, with a good sword. Let your pet go first into unknown rooms, don't eat corpses you can't identify, and when you're in trouble, #pray — your god will usually help if you haven't prayed recently. Read the messages at the top; NetHack tells you almost everything, but only once.

The game is the NetHack DevTeam's own source, compiled to WebAssembly by the neth4ck project and released under the NetHack General Public License. The window port that draws the map and menus and reads your keys is written for this site. NetHack's built-in help files live in the game's data archive, which this build doesn't expose to the help viewer, so a few help pages show a short notice instead.

faq.q: Is this the real NetHack or a clone?
faq.a: The real one: NetHack 3.6.7, the last 3.6 release, built from the official source to WebAssembly. The rules, monsters, items and every special level are the originals.

faq.q: Where is my save kept?
faq.a: In your browser's IndexedDB storage for this site, under the name you chose. Clearing site data deletes it, and it doesn't move between browsers or devices.

faq.q: Can I play with tiles instead of letters?
faq.a: Not yet — this version draws the classic coloured characters.

faq.q: Is NetHack free?
faq.a: Yes. NetHack has always been free software under the NetHack General Public License, which allows it to be shared and hosted as long as the licence and source stay available.

intro: 2048 is the sliding-tile puzzle Gabriele Cirulli wrote over a weekend in March 2014 and released as open source. This is the original game, running the author's own code — slide the tiles, merge matching numbers and try to build the 2048 tile.

sections.html: Use the arrow keys, or swipe on a touch screen. Every move slides all the tiles as far as they will go in that direction. When two tiles with the same number meet, they merge into one tile with their sum. After each move a new 2 or 4 appears in an empty square. You win when you make a 2048 tile, and you can keep going after that; the game ends when the board is full and no move is possible.

Pick a corner and keep your largest tile there. Fill that tile's row in descending order, and avoid the one direction that would pull the big tile out of its corner unless you have no other move. Most games are lost by a single careless swipe, not by bad luck.

Cirulli published 2048 under the MIT licence, which allows anyone to copy and host it. The files here are his, unmodified, and the game itself makes no requests to any other site. Your best score is stored in your own browser.

sections.h: How it works & what to expect
sections.html:
The game is the SuperTux team's official WebAssembly release, hosted here unchanged. It is big: about 250 MB of levels, graphics and music are downloaded the first time you play, so start it on Wi-Fi and give it a minute or two. After that your browser keeps it.

SuperTux opens as a page of its own, not inside this one. It runs on several threads, and browsers only allow that on a page that is isolated from other sites — which a game framed inside another page cannot be. Use your browser's Back button to return here.

It needs WebGL and a reasonably recent computer. It is not a good fit for phones or for low-memory Chromebooks.

Use the arrow keys to move, Space to jump and Ctrl to run or throw fireballs once you have a fire flower; the down arrow ducks. Every key can be changed under Options → Setup Keyboard. Choose Start Game → Story Mode to begin on Icy Island; the Level Editor on the main menu works in the browser too.

SuperTux is free software. Its code is under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or later, and most of its artwork, levels and music are under Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike. Nothing here is a demo or a first episode: it is the whole game, as the project released it.

faq.q: Why does it open as a separate page?
